articles.title: Ronald Lauder, a Billionaire G.O.P. Backer, Closes His Wallet
articles.text:
Supported by
Times Exclusive
Ronald Lauder, a Billionaire G.O.P. Backer, Closes His Wallet
Ronald S. Lauder, a major funder of conservative political causes, has not given a single dollar this year to Republicans in his home state, and his super PAC has gone idle.
For decades, Ronald S. Lauder, the billionaire cosmetics heir and philanthropist, has been something like a one-man bank for Republicans in New York.
He personally funded a campaign to impose term limits in New York City, helped pay for a lawsuit to overturn the state’s gerrymandered congressional map and, just four years ago, plowed close to $13 million into races that helped Republicans flip the House.
Now, in the middle of another crucial midterm election year, Mr. Lauder, 82, appears to have abruptly closed his political checkbook, and the ramifications for the conservative movement he has nurtured in his home state could be significant.
He has yet to make a single donation to Republicans in his home state this year, according to campaign finance records. The super PAC he long maintained to advance Republican candidates and causes is also sitting idle.
And behind the scenes, Mr. Lauder has quietly dismissed a stable of well-paid advisers, ad makers and other consultants who regularly reported to his personal office in the Estée Lauder headquarters overlooking Central Park in Manhattan. Some had been with Mr. Lauder since 1989 when he ran his own quixotic race for mayor.
His motivation is not entirely clear. Three associates said that Mr. Lauder recently confided in them, saying that his adult children have stepped in to try to reduce his lavish spending on politics, art and philanthropy and suggesting reluctantly that he could not spend what he once did. The associates pointed to public securities filings showing that his stake in the family business, Estée Lauder, has lost at least $1.2 billion in value as the stock plummeted 77 percent from its 2021 high.
A person close to the Lauder family did not dispute that Mr. Lauder’s political spending was being curtailed, but said it was not because of a financial pinch.
Rather, the person said that he and his adult children had agreed that he would simplify the reach of his activities — involving extensive travel, large paid staff and public speeches — as he prepared for the last years of his life in order to prioritize art and philanthropic projects that could secure his legacy.
The New York Times pieced together this account of one of New York City’s most publicly engaged donors and philanthropists by examining public campaign finance records and corporate disclosures by Estée Lauder, and interviewing more than a dozen of his associates. Most insisted on anonymity to avoid crossing him.
Mr. Lauder himself did not respond to a detailed list of questions from The Times about his financial position or decision making.
In a written statement, he said that he had used political giving and philanthropy over the years to “strengthen” the city, adding, “I intend to continue dedicating my time, resources and energy to advancing those democratic principles and to ensuring that New York remains a place where people, families, businesses and communities can thrive.”
Some Republicans are holding out hope that Mr. Lauder might still involve himself in this year’s races. But Gerard Kassar, the chairman of the New York Conservative Party, said he had been advised by Allen Roth, a longtime Lauder lieutenant who recently left, that the billionaire “got to a certain age that his family and him all decided he wasn’t going to be as active the way he has been.”
Mr. Kassar said he did not know anything about Mr. Lauder’s personal finances, but was led to believe he would no longer be a major funder.
“Can anyone replace him in New York financially?” Mr. Kassar said. “The simple answer is no.”
Edward F. Cox, Mr. Kassar’s counterpart at the state Republican Party and a longtime friend of the Lauder family, declined to comment.
There is little doubt that Mr. Lauder is still enormously wealthy. He owns one of the world’s most respected private art collections, a Gulfstream with custom Hermès interiors and compounds in Palm Beach and the Hamptons. Forbes estimates that he and both of his adult daughters are worth billions of dollars.
There are signs that Mr. Lauder is taking other significant actions that could reverberate far beyond the political world. Many of the maneuvers, including giving up his Estée Lauder board seat, are consistent with the kind of estate planning typical of a wealthy person of his age.
But some of the moves he initiated over the past few years have also either generated substantial cash or offloaded tens of millions of dollars in future obligations at a time when the family business had taken a sharp downward turn.
In the most high-profile case, Mr. Lauder announced in May that his beloved Neue Galerie, the Upper East Side museum he founded to showcase the culture of prewar Austria and Germany, would be merging with the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
Both sides framed the blockbuster merger as a way to preserve the museum well beyond Mr. Lauder’s lifetime and strengthen the Met’s collection. But it would also be likely to save Mr. Lauder millions of dollars a year that he contributes to covering its operating expenses, according to the organization’s financial disclosures.
Mr. Lauder also recently announced that he would leave the presidency of the World Jewish Congress, an international federation of Jewish groups, where he has been the major funder and leader for two decades.
At the same time, Mr. Lauder, who began collecting as a teenager — real estate, planes and, most of all, art — has quietly been selling at a notable clip.
In late 2023, as the Estée Lauder stock slide accelerated, he sold a Philip Johnson-designed home in Manhattan for $20 million in an off-market deal. In late 2024, he sold 30 acres of land to the Town of East Hampton’s preservation fund for $56 million, and put his collection of World War II fighter planes on the market, according to an aviation enthusiasts’ website.
Mr. Lauder’s retrenchment has played out at a time of significant change for his storied family. His older brother, the businessman and philanthropist Leonard A. Lauder, died last year. His son-in-law, Kevin M. Warsh, was recently nominated to the chairmanship of the Federal Reserve by President Trump, a longtime friend of Ronald Lauder.
While Leonard Lauder spent his career leading the family business, Ronald Lauder carved out a path as an independent investor, philanthropist, art collector and political player, serving as a U.S. ambassador under Ronald Reagan.
Those pursuits were expensive, and in addition to outright selling his stock, Mr. Lauder long made a practice of using shares in the family business as collateral for bank loans and other financial transactions to help fund it all. (Estée Lauder’s most recent annual federal securities filing disclosed that he had pledged nearly all his remaining shares to a bank.)
The maneuver is popular among people who derive their wealth from stocks as a way to generate cash from their holdings without selling them and paying taxes. It would have had little downside when the company’s stock was going up in value. Estée Lauder shares peaked, at the end of 2021, at around $370 a share.
But there can be risks if the stock used as collateral loses considerable value. If the assets’ values fall far enough, a lender may ask the borrower to repay part of the loan or pledge more assets to maintain it.
The terms of Mr. Lauder’s borrowing are not specified in the Estée Lauder disclosures. As of this week, the stock was trading at around $85 a share.
The person close to the Lauder family conceded that the stock price’s slide could limit Mr. Lauder’s overall capital, but asserted that he did not have a meaningful liquidity problem. (The person declined to share financial records that would substantiate the claim.)

articles.title: Tick-borne 'rabbit fever' spreads with cases reported near major metro area
articles.text:
Health officials on Long Island are warning residents about a rare but potentially serious tick-borne illness.
Three probable cases of tularemia — also known as "rabbit fever" — have been confirmed by the Suffolk County Department of Health Services (SCDHS).
"SCDHS currently has three probable cases of tularemia this year," the agency said in a statement provided to local outlets. "Confirmation of a tularemia diagnosis requires a combination of laboratory testing and fulfillment of specific clinical or epidemiologic criteria. The laboratory testing to confirm a tularemia diagnosis may take several weeks."
NO CURE, NO VACCINE: EXPERTS WARN OF RARE BOURBON VIRUS AFTER FIRST NY CASE
One case involved a 9-year-old patient who was bitten by a tick while playing outside, according to NBC4 New York. After the tick was removed, he later developed high fever, severe head and neck pain, swollen lymph nodes/glands, body aches and extreme fatigue.
After multiple doctor visits and nearly a month of illness, an infectious disease specialist diagnosed the boy with tularemia.
Although the family's yard is home to wild rabbits, the patient's mother said he never handled the animals. Doctors believe infected ticks likely fed on the rabbits before biting the boy, transmitting the bacteria, according to reports.
What to know about rabbit fever
Caused by the bacteria Francisella tularensis, the disease commonly infects rabbits, hares and rodents. However, it is zoonotic, which means it can spread from animals to humans.
The bacteria is a "tier-1 select agent," a classification given to agents and toxins that "present the greatest risk of deliberate misuse with significant potential for mass casualties or devastating effects to the economy, critical infrastructure or public confidence, and pose a severe threat to public health and safety," per the CDC.
TICK BITE ER VISITS HIT HIGHEST SEASONAL LEVEL IN YEARS AS DOCTORS WARN OF DISEASE SURGE
Although tularemia remains rare, with 196 U.S. cases reported in 2023, the disease has become more common in recent years. CDC surveillance found 2,462 cases between 2011 and 2022 — a 56% increase in incidence compared with the previous decade (2001–2010).
Daniel Ruderfer, M.D., chief of the Division of Pediatric Infectious Diseases at Hackensack Meridian K. Hovnanian Children's Hospital in New Jersey, believes that the increase in cases is mostly due to improved microbiology detection methods.
"The traditional method of confirming cases has historically been via growth in culture and antibody testing," he previously told Fox News Digital.
"However, newer detection methods, such as PCR testing, are likely a major contributor to the increase in reported cases."

Humans can contract the disease through bites from deer flies or ticks, contact with infected animals, or exposure to contaminated water or aerosols, the same source stated.
Symptoms of tularemia can vary depending on the type of disease. General symptoms include chills, headache, malaise, fatigue, anorexia, myalgia, chest discomfort, cough, severe sore throat, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain, according to Ruderfer.
"Depending on the location of the infected bit or scratch, people can develop localized lymphadenopathy (enlarged lymph nodes) and a cutaneous ulcer at the infection site," he said.
"Other manifestations include conjuctivitis, pneumonia and potentially even bloodstream infections."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The death rate from the disease is typically low, less than 2%, but the CDC noted that it can be as high as 24% in rare, severe cases.
Tularemia can be treated with antibiotics, but no vaccine is currently available.

"The infection is absolutely dangerous and potentially life-threatening if not treated with appropriate antibiotics," said Ruderfer.
Those most at risk include children between 5 and 9 years of age, older men, American Indian and Alaskan Native people, and those living in central U.S. states, according to the report.

The general population is not at an "obvious" risk for infection unless they come into physical contact with an infected rabbit, tick or deer fly, the expert noted.

Those who hunt or interact routinely with rabbits should see a doctor if they develop any concerning symptoms, he advised.
"Many factors might contribute to the higher risk for tularemia in this population, including the concentration of Native American reservations in central states and sociocultural or occupational activities that might increase contact with infected wildlife or arthropods," the CDC wrote.

articles.title: WNBA fan goes viral for half-court shot horror show that left him sprawled on the court
articles.text:
Few things in sports can get a fan's nerves up like being told you get to take a half-court shot at an NBA or WNBA game for cash or a car.
Sure, you could, by some miracle, make the shot, but you're more likely to embarrass yourself in front of an arena full of people... at least the ones who are still in their seats and aren't in line for a beer or the bathroom.
But, at least we can all be sure that if you take a shot, the odds of it being a worse display than one put on by a Portland Fire fan over the weekend are very, very low.
The Fire (whose logo I only just realized is a flaming rose. Seriously, I've had an easier time decoding death metal band logos) have a half-court shot competition according to their website. It's sponsored by Toyota, meaning that draining the shot earns you a brand new Toyota.
Hopefully a Land Cruiser. Those are cool.
One fan got this golden opportunity on Sunday when the Fire took on the Los Angeles Sparks and... well, let's just say that Portland area Toyota dealers were not sweating it on this one.
Oh, dear God...
ATLANTA BRAVES FAN TAUNTS THE FREEZE WITH A BLOWN KISS AND GETS PASSED IN SPECTACULAR FASHION
Rule No. 1 of half-court shots should be that whatever you do, your biggest goal is to at least hit the backboard. I'd argue it's much better to airmail that ball into the club level seats than it is to barely get it past the free throw line.
That's a rough look as it is, but imagine putting every last drop of mustard you have on the ball to the point that you go scrawling across that flaming rose logo (seriously, did anyone else not pick up on that at first?). That tells the entire crowd in attendance you gave it your all... which is normally good, but that's not enough "all."
The big winner in all of this is that guy's glasses. Talk about a snug fit. Those things were on there!
That was maybe the only thing that went right for him. If those specs had gone clattering across the hardwood, I think he would've had to change his name, move out of Portland, and start rooting for a new WNBA team.

Luckily for him, he wasn't the only loser as the Fire fell to the Sparks that night 106-101.
articles.summary: A Portland Fire fan's half-court shot attempt during the WNBA game against the Los Angeles Sparks barely cleared the free throw line area.

The biological male, who came out as trans in October 2021, led the league in both categories. It was as season unlike any the Ligue 2 had ever seen.
With those numbers, the WNBA should be knocking down Tétart's door, right?
"If they contact me, I won't say no. But you have to be realistic: I'm old, and there are far better players than me!" the overly humble 34-year-old Tétart told OutKick in French over Instagram direct messages on Monday.
Far better? Are you sure?
Tétart's season was so dominant that French media was stunned when the shredded center didn't win league MVP honors. The season was still good enough to win Player of the Year, Defensive Player of the Year and Domestic Player of the Year.
Woke WNBA fans swear there's no clear and present trans danger to biological women. They swear this is some sort of delusion cooked up by MAGA.

Former WNBA player Audrey Sauret, who's French, spoke out in April after the MVP drama and sounded a warning to leagues around the world as to what's coming if they don't protect biological females.

During a March game that should've been a trans showdown, Tétart had 21 points and 30 rebounds, which was a new league record, breaking the previous record of 25 rebounds (Tétart held that record, as well), but Pautou didn't play.
The question we had for Tétart was simple: Would you ever consider trying out for the inclusive WNBA? The trans scoring and rebounding machine seemed confused at first before realizing we were 100% serious.
"Obviously, it's a childhood dream just like for any female basketball player, but unfortunately, it's not possible," the French native wrote back.
Wait a minute, why not? The WNBA is inclusive. What are we missing here?
"The league, yes. The country, no, haha," Tétart fired back while hinting at some sort of problem with Donald Trump's presidency.
When pressed on what would need to change politically in the U.S., Tétart stopped playing games with me, finally admitting that if a WNBA call came, it would be time to talk business: "I won't say no."
As for Sophie Cunningham's stance that biological males need to stay out of women's sports, I gave Tétart a chance to respond. "Aucun," the French stat stuffer replied.

articles.title: The scam text test: Spot danger before you tap
articles.text:
Your phone buzzes. The text reads, "Your package is delayed. Confirm your address here." A little later, it's a text message about an unpaid toll, suspicious bank activity or an account that will be locked unless you act now.
That's how scam texts work. They don't always look wild or obviously fake. They look routine, urgent and easy to deal with in a hurry. The good news: You don't need to memorize every scam. You just need a quick way to test suspicious messages before you tap. Here's the simple scam text test to run before you click, pay or share anything.
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist
Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?", has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE SHINYHUNTERS SEXTORTION EMAIL USES CARNIVAL BREACH DATA
The scam text test
If a text asks you to click, pay, verify, sign in or fix a problem, run through these checks first.
1) Was I expecting this?
Are you actually waiting for that package? Do you use that bank? Did you recently drive on a toll road? If the answer is no, treat the message as suspicious. Even if the answer is yes, don't assume it's real. Scammers rely on coincidence. They send thousands of similar messages knowing that some recipients will be waiting for a package or use the company being impersonated.
2) Is it trying to rush me?
Urgency is one of the biggest red flags. Watch for phrases like:
- Act now
- Final warning
- Verify immediately
- Avoid penalties
- Account suspended
A real company may send an urgent alert, but scammers use pressure to stop you from checking whether the message is legitimate. Take a breath before responding. A few extra minutes spent verifying the message can prevent days or weeks of dealing with a stolen account.
3) Does the link look off?
Before tapping, check for:
- Misspelled brand names
- Extra words or random characters
- Shortened links
- Web addresses that look close to the real one but aren't exact
- Domains that have nothing to do with the company named in the message
Even if the address looks legitimate, avoid opening links in unexpected texts. Scammers can disguise links or create convincing copies of real websites. Verify the message through the company's official app or a website you type in yourself.
4) Is the message generic or awkward?
Many scam texts use vague greetings, odd wording, awkward punctuation or slightly incorrect brand names. You might see a message addressed to "Dear customer" instead of your name. It may refer to a package without showing an order number or claim to come from a bank without identifying the account involved. Good grammar doesn't guarantee a message is safe. Scammers now use artificial intelligence to write more convincing messages. Still, sloppy wording and missing details remain warning signs.
5) Is it asking for information no company should request by text?
Be skeptical of any text asking for:
- Passwords
- Card numbers
- Bank login details
- Social Security numbers
- Immediate payment
- One-time codes that you must send, share or read back
Legitimate companies may send you a one-time verification code. However, a bank, government agency or customer service representative should never ask you to give that code to someone else. Anyone who asks for your code may be trying to take control of your account.
6) Can I verify it without using the text?
This is the most important step. Instead of using the link or phone number in the message:
- Open the official app
- Type the company's website address manually
- Call the number printed on your card or bill
- Use a phone number found on the company's official website
If the issue is real, you should still be able to find it through one of those trusted channels.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
What scam texts usually look like
Scam texts often fall into a few familiar categories.
Fake delivery alerts
These messages claim a package was delayed, an address needs to be corrected or a small shipping fee must be paid. The link may lead to afake postal or delivery websitethat collects your card information, password or home address.
Fake bank alerts
These texts claim someone used your card, your account has been locked or you must verify a transaction immediately. The message may include a phone number connecting you to a scammer pretending to work for the bank.
Fake toll notices
Toll scams claim you owe a small amount and will face a larger penalty if you don't pay immediately. The amount is often low enough to make paying seem easier than investigating. The payment page then steals your financial information.
Fake account warnings
These messages claim your email, payment app, streaming service or social media account will be suspended. They direct you to a fake login page designed to capture your username and password. These scams work because each message sounds plausible. The goal is to make you react first and think later.
What to do if you already tapped
Don't panic, but act quickly.
If you clicked a link
- Close the page
- Don't download anything
- Don't enter any information
- Clear the page from your browser history
- Watch for unusual pop-ups, downloads or account alerts
Simply opening a phishing page doesn't always mean your information was stolen. The risk increases if you entered information, downloaded a file or approved a permission request.
If you entered a password
- Change the password immediately
- Change it on any other account where you reused it
- Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA)
- Review recent account activity
- Sign out of devices you don't recognize
Use a different password for every important account. A password manager can create and store strong passwords so one stolen login doesn't give scammers access to everything else.
If you shared a one-time code
Change the affected account's password immediately and check whether a new device, email address or phone number was added. Contact the company through its official app, website or phone number. Tell the representative that someone may have gained access to your account.
If you entered payment details
- Contact your bank or card issuer immediately
- Ask whether the card should be locked or replaced
- Review your recent transactions
- Monitor the account for unauthorized charges
- Consider adding transaction alerts
Report any charges you don't recognize as soon as possible.
HOTEL WI-FI PHISHING ATTACK TARGETS MICROSOFT LOGINS
If you entered your Social Security number
Visit IdentityTheft.gov to create a recovery plan. You may also want to place a fraud alert or security freeze on your credit files. A credit freeze can prevent criminals from opening many types of new accounts in your name.
If you downloaded something
- Run a security scan
- Remove suspicious apps, programs or files
- Review recently installed apps
- Check for unfamiliar device permissions
- Update your operating system and security software
Avoid entering sensitive information on the device until you are confident it is secure.
Report the scam text
After securing your accounts:
- Use your phone's Report Junk or Report Spam option
- Forward the message to 7726, which spells SPAM
- Block the sender
- Delete the message
- Report the scam to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov
Reporting scam texts helps phone carriers and government agencies identify active campaigns.
How antivirus software can help
Good habits are your first line of defense, but strong antivirus software can add another layer of protection. Some security tools can warn you about suspicious links, phishing websites and malicious do

articles.title: Paul Finebaum’s proclamation about Alabama coach Kalen DeBoer reignites college football ‘culture fit’ debate
articles.text:
I mentioned it a while back, but August is the only time of year when almost every college football fanbase feels like their team has a chance to win it all.
Hope does indeed spring eternal every summer, but there are still plenty of programs who realistically have no shot at even making a College Football Playoff appearance.
One juggernaut who has historically been among the "haves" rather than the "have nots" is the Alabama Crimson Tide, but according to college football commentator Paul Finebaum, Bama's days of owning the lion's share of championship trophies may have come to an abrupt halt.
And it's all thanks to the man they hired to fill the team-issued polo previously worn by Nick Saban.
DID ALABAMA DOOM THEMSELVES TO MEDIOCRITY WITH KALEN DEBOER EXTENSION?
"I'm selling that," Finebaum said on Crane & Co. when asked if he would "buy or sell" Alabama coach Kalen DeBoer winning a natty while in Tuscaloosa. "I'll spare you the 'I think Kalen DeBoer is a good football coach.' I think everybody does. The question is, 'is he going to win a championship at Alabama?' And my answer is no."
Finebaum goes on to call the "culture fit" between DeBoer and Bama "okay," and says Alabama is a unique job where sometimes really good football coaches don't necessarily win titles due to factors that go far beyond the painted lines of Bryant Denny Stadium.
"In the last 60 years, only three people have won national championships, two of them happen to be the greatest coach of all-time on the day they retired," Finebaum stated. "At Alabama, you can be unique, you can be different, but Kalen DeBoer, to me, just doesn't have the right ingredients to win the title there."
'HOT SEAT RANKINGS' FOR ALL 16 SEC COACHES AS BEGINNING OF 2026 COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON DRAWS NEARER
It's interesting to hear Finebaum say that DeBoer doesn't have the right "ingredients" to win at Bama, but if you know what he means by that, it makes a ton of sense.
"Ingredients," in this instance, doesn't refer to talent on the field, because DeBoer and his staff haven't exactly been lacking in that department.
In the three full offseasons that DeBoer has been the head coach at Alabama, his average recruiting class ranking according to the 247Sports composite has been 2.5.
Every coach in America can only dream of averaging a top-three recruiting class every year they've been at their current school, but it's more than just a talent issue.
IF YOU BELIEVE ALABAMA WASN'T RECRUITING JEREMIAH SMITH, YOU DON'T UNDERSTAND RECRUITING
As Finebaum mentioned, the "culture fit" wasn't right from the start between DeBoer and his current employer, and though that may sound like a nebulous excuse, there's some real weight behind it.
"He's capable of winning it elsewhere," Finebaum reasoned. "He came within a reasonable chance of winning it at Washington. I think he could probably have won one at Michigan. Alabama's different."
For those who don't remember, DeBoer was rolling while coaching the Washington Huskies.
In his two seasons in the Pacific Northwest, DeBoer had two top-ten finishes and a national championship appearance under his belt.
BY ADDING ED ORGERON TO STAFF, LANE KIFFIN AND LSU ADDRESS KEY FLAW FROM PREVIOUS REGIME
Even before he arrived at the ranks of the Power 4, DeBoer was a noted winner, capturing three NAIA National Championships while at Sioux Falls and guiding Fresno State to a nine-win regular season in just his second year there.
The point is, DeBoer didn't just forget how to coach the moment his plane touched down in Tuscaloosa, and it's not like he's been an abject failure for the Tide either.
Averaging ten wins a year and making a CFP appearance would be welcomed at 99% of schools in the country.
But as Finebaum said so poignantly, "Alabama is different."
CURT CIGNETTI REVEALS HOW WORKING FOR NICK SABAN CHANGED EVERYTHING: 'EVERY DAY WAS 4TH-AND-1'
It's the same reason a guy like Brian Kelly, a coach who went 145-61 in his three FBS stops prior to landing in Baton Rouge, "failed" at LSU.
Kelly is not a bad coach or even an average coach, but he didn't understand the culture and expectations that come with being the Tigers' head coach.
Will DeBoer prove everyone wrong and win a title at Bama? I can't say for sure.
As long as they keep recruiting at their current pace, a coach like DeBoer has a chance.
WHAT DOES A REALISTICALLY SUCCESSFUL FIRST YEAR LOOK LIKE FOR HEAD COACH LANE KIFFIN AT LSU?
But I also wouldn't be shocked to see him looking for a job in two to three years either.
Programs like Alabama and LSU have one goal and one goal only: to win a national championship.
And sometimes, even that isn't enough to save your job (see: Ed Orgeron).
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
DeBoer will be judged by the trophy case he assembles while coaching the Crimson Tide, and right now, that sucker is looking a little empty.
articles.summary: Paul Finebaum says Kalen DeBoer lacks the right ingredients to win a national championship at Alabama despite averaging top-three recruiting classes.

articles.title: Southern California Edison equipment blamed for 2025 Eaton Fire in Los Angeles
articles.text:
Southern California Edison equipment blamed for 2025 Eaton Fire in Los Angeles
Los Angeles fire officials say the deadly 2025 Eaton Fire was caused by Southern California Edison equipment
The deadly 2025 Eaton Fire in Los Angeles was caused by Southern California Edison equipment, fire officials say.
Los Angeles County Fire officials said in a report released Tuesday that the cause of the fire that killed 19 people and destroyed or damaged more than 9,000 homes and businesses was a tower that was not in service.
“After 18 months of thorough review of all evidence, alongside retained electrical and metallurgical experts, the investigation concluded that the cause of the wildfire conflagration was due to the electrical arcing events that took place on the out-of-service Southern California Edison (SCE) tower,” the agency said in a statement.
The Eaton Fire was one of two blazes that broke out on Jan. 7, 2025. It took firefighters nearly a month to extinguish the blaze, which scorched 22 square miles (57 square kilometers). SoCal Edison has claimed in lawsuits earlier this year that Los Angeles County agencies failed to send timely evacuation warnings to residents in east and west Altadena. Eighteen of the 19 people who died in the fire lived in west Altadena.
The utility also has claimed water agencies, including Pasadena Water and Power, did not provide enough water as the fire spread, leaving firefighters with limited resources. Los Angeles County declined to comment about the latest court filings.
The Eaton Fire burned at the same time as the Palisades Fire, the most destructive blaze in Los Angeles to date and among the five worst in California’s history. The blaze killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 homes and buildings in Pacific Palisades. The fire ripped through hillside neighborhoods, destroying mansions with spectacular ocean views.
articles.summary: Los Angeles fire officials say the deadly 2025 Eaton Fire was caused by Southern California Edison equipment

articles.title: Senate Judiciary Committee advances Blanche's nomination for attorney general
articles.text:
Senate Judiciary Committee advances Todd Blanche's nomination for attorney general
He won over two key GOP senators by rescinding the "Anti-Weaponization Fund."
The Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday voted to advance acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's nomination to permanently lead the Department of Justice.
Blanche advanced in a 12-10 party line vote. All Republicans voted in favor of him, while all Democrats voted against.
Republican Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis ultimately supported Blanche after securing an agreement that clarified the scope of President Donald Trump's IRS immunity deal and formally rescinded the administration's so-called $1.8 billion "Anti-Weaponization Fund."
Despite the fact that the agreement reached has no language preventing the resurrection of the controversial fund under a different name or method, Cornyn said the DOJ has been "consistent" about their assertions that the fund is dead.
"And of course, I expect them to live up to that in any future litigation," Cornyn said in remarks on the Senate panel ahead of the vote.
Tillis also said the agreement reached with Blanche satisfies his concerns.
"I believe that we have addressed the concerns that I have. The first one I called the 'payout pot for punks.' I've never liked this 1776 fund. It made no sense to me, and I thought it was an insult to the police officers and the people that defended us on January the 6th. It's done. It's been rescinded, and I am satisfied," Tillis said.
Tillis said that both sides on the aisle "have a problem" when it comes to malicious prosecution. He said he hopes to see a "bending of the curve of this absurdity" when Blanche is confirmed.
Ahead of the vote, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley thanked Cornyn and Tillis for their work securing the agreement. He said many senators shared their concerns.
"Formally rescinding the fund and clarifying the scope of release of claims has put this issue to bed once and for all," Grassley said.
Democratic Sen. Chris Coons took a different view on the so-called "Anti-Weaponization Fund" than his Republican colleagues, arguing that Blanche's willingness to go along with its creation in the first place should disqualify him from the attorney general job.
"In my view, we never should have gotten to this place. As acting attorney general, when asked by the president to do something plainly unethical and corrupt, Mr. Blanche should have simply said no. He did not do that, and I pressed him in his confirmation hearing whether he even tried to talk President Trump out of this widely rejected plan, and he refused to answer," Coons said.
During the hearing, Blanche responded to Coons' questions, saying he was not simply a "yes man" in giving Trump counsel.
"I will say that President Trump trusts me to give him counsel. Counsel does not mean I'm a 'yes man.' And that's true in my case, like it should be in any attorneys general case," Blanche said during his confirmation hearing.
Several Democrats on the panel raised a number of concerns about Blanche.
"Today I think is a sad and embarrassing day for this committee, as it looks like, on a party line vote, we are going to advance out of this committee probably the most discreditable person ever to seek the office of attorney general of the United States," Democratic Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse said.
Democratic Sen. Cory Booker in a lengthy speech, warned that the country was in "dangerous waters" with Blanche.
"This man is not our lawyer. He is not America's lawyer. He is about to become Trump's sword against his adversaries and shield against any scrutiny," Booker said.
What's next for Blanche's nomination?
Blanche's nomination is now ready for consideration on the Senate floor.
Unless there is an agreement to speed things along, the soonest the Senate can take a procedural vote on Blanche's nomination is Friday. That would set up a final confirmation vote sometime on Saturday.
Though Tillis and Cornyn were the most closely watched Republican votes on the Senate Judiciary Committee, there remains other GOP senators who have raised concerns about Blanche.
With Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell still absent from Congress, Blanche will ultimately only be able to lose the support of two Republicans when his nomination comes up for a vote on the Senate floor.
articles.summary: The Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday voted to advance acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's nomination to permanently lead the Department of Justice.

articles.title: What to know about the victims of the In-N-Out Burger shooting
articles.text:
What to know about the victims of the In-N-Out Burger shooting
"She lit up a room with her bright smile," said the family of Ashley Garibay.
Two of the three victims killed in a shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Idaho have been identified by their families, including one who was described as someone who "lit up a room with her bright smile" and another who had found sobriety after overcoming the death of his newlywed wife.
Christopher Claunch and Ashley Garibay were killed during a shooting rampage on Saturday at one of the fast-food chain's eateries in Twin Falls, Idaho, their families said.
The suspected shooter, identified as 24-year-old Chad Williams, died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound after two armed Good Samaritans returned fire, according to police.
A third victim who was killed has not yet been publicly identified.
Seven other people were wounded in the shooting, including two who were critically injured, authorities said.
Ashley Garibay
Family members said Ashley Garibay worked as an In-N-Out Burger associate in California, but traveled to Twin Falls to help train the staff at the chain's newly opened restaurant.
“We are heartbroken and devastated by the loss of Ashley – a devoted daughter, sister, auntie, cousin and friend – whose life was taken from us far too soon," Garibay's family said in a statement.
Relatives said Garibay's landed her first job working at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Stockton, California, and "fell in love with it."
"She proudly traveled to open new stores, and her dream was to one day manage an In-N-Out store. She was passionate about serving Customers and left this world doing what she loved to do," the family's statement said.
Garibay was described by her family as "a devoted daughter, sister, auntie, cousin and friend -- whose life was taken from us far too soon."
"Ashley was an amazing, beautiful soul who loved living life," her family said. "She was adventurous, outgoing, smart and driven, never letting obstacles get in her way. She lit up a room with her bright smile and a laugh that was contagious. She was a friend to all, and no matter what difficulties she was facing, she always found a way to help others find the light in the darkness."
Christopher Claunch
A California native, 59-year-old Christopher Claunch fell in love with Idaho and decided to move there three decades ago, according to his sister, Kimberly Castaneda.
Castaneda told The New York Times that her brother worked at the Renaissance Ranch Recovery Center in Rupert, Idaho.
Claunch had found sobriety two years ago after struggling with alcoholism for many years, his sister told the Times.
She told The New York Times that her brother's first wife died in a car crash just three months after they were married and that "he had always hurt from that loss."
After moving to Idaho 30 years ago, Claunch met his partner of 25 years, Teresa Sperry, whom he shared a home with.
Sperry told the Times that Claunch loved traveling, cooking and the outdoors.
Castaneda said her brother would make it a point to eat at an In-N-Out Burger every time he visited the California, where the fast-food chain was founded and where it's restaurants are primarily located.
When the In-N-Out Burger in Twin Falls opened last month, Castaneda said her brother told her he was looking forward to going there, but planned to wait, "knowing the hype would only cause long lines."
"You have no idea how surprised I was when I found out he was there," Castaneda told the Times.
ABC News' Chris Looft and Karem Inal contributed to this report.
articles.summary: Two of the three victims killed in a shooting at an Idaho In-N-Out Burger restaurant on Saturday have been identified by their families.

articles.title: ICE arrested 51K individuals in July, highest in a single month in DHS history
articles.text:
ICE arrests hit record high in July as enforcement quietly ramps up
The Department of Homeland Security has been ramping up arrests.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested 51,000 individuals in July, according to sources familiar with the data.
The arrests are the largest in a single month in DHS history, according to data.
It comes as ICE is ramping up arrests at airports -- with ICE arresting over 30 people at airports in July, agency data shows.
Those being detained in some cases do not have criminal records and have valid work authorization or parole documents, according to one immigration attorney that spoke with ABC News.
The Department of Homeland Security has not responded to ABC News' request for comment about the numbers.
In June, DHS announced that the total number of deportations so far this fiscal year is 356,389, according to the numbers posted by ICE.
ICE has quietly been increasing their operations around the country, according to a law enforcement source.
Some allies of President Donald Trump say the numbers should be released in full and the enforcement doesn't go far enough.
"The point is the numbers remain wildly disproportionately low to the scale of illegals let in by Biden and the promise of mass deportation," Mike Howell, the president of the Trump-aligned Oversight Project, told ABC News. "The numbers will stay low until worksite enforcement is the central pillar of the strategy. I'm very worried about the amnesty lobby continuing to use inflated deportation statistics to push for a grand compromise and sell out. That's why I'm suing DHS for real data and will keep doing it until I don't have to."
"DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country," a DHS spokesperson said in a statement to ABC News. "Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this. This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport."
articles.summary: The Department of Homeland Security has been ramping up arrests.

articles.title: Some Haitian immigrants in Ohio told to report to ICE and given ankle monitors
articles.text:
Some Haitian immigrants in Ohio told to report to ICE and given ankle monitors
The Trump administration last month ended TPS for about 350,000 Haitians.
Hundreds of Haitian immigrants in Ohio who had Temporary Protected Status have been summoned by the Department of Homeland Security for in-person "check-ins" with the agency, where some have been fitted with ankle monitors, immigration advocates tell ABC News.
The move from the government comes after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in June that the Trump administration could end TPS for about 350,000 Haitians, as part of the administration's ongoing immigration crackdown.
Steve Foster, the immigration policy coordinator for the Institute for Justice and Democracy in Haiti, said "Haitians with TPS, regardless of whether they have a pending asylum claim, have gotten a 'DHS Call-In Letter' to appear at ICE offices in person."
Some have been given ankle monitors and future court dates, Foster said.
Viles Dorsainvil, executive director of a Haitian support group in Springfield, Ohio, confirmed the government's effort to call Haitians in Ohio with TPS into ICE offices and fit some of them with ankle monitors.
"We are just helping these folks to go to this appointment, and when they get there, they interview them and eventually put [an] ankle monitor on them," Dorsainvil said.
TPS status, established by the 1952 Immigration and Nationality Act, provides work authorization and protection from deportation if a foreign country is deemed by the government to be unsafe because of armed conflict, natural disaster, or "extraordinary and temporary conditions."
In a statement, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said, "Temporary Protected Status is exactly that -- temporary. For too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent."
"What we would say now is it's closing time, which means you don't have to go home, but you can't stay here," the statement said.
Dorsainvil said that some TPS holders have lost their work permits, while others who have pending asylum cases still have valid work authorization.
"There is so much anxiety, and they are fearful, and they are uncertain when it comes to what they should do next," he said.
articles.summary: Hundreds of Haitian immigrants in Ohio who had Temporary Protected Status have been summoned by the ICE for in-person "check-ins," immigration advocates say.

articles.title: Pirro meets with Trump at White House amid questions about her future
articles.text:
Pirro meets with Trump at White House amid questions about her future
Trump said she "folded like an umbrella" in dropping Reflecting Pool charges.
U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro met with President Donald Trump at the White House Monday afternoon amid questions about her future, sources familiar with the matter told ABC News.
The meeting came after Trump said Pirro "choked" and "folded like an umbrella" in dropping charges last week against those charged with damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment about the meeting. When asked about the future of Pirro's job, a White House official referred ABC News to Trump's comments earlier in the Oval Office in which he was critical of her decision to drop the case.
Trump has privately mused to aides about whether he should fire Pirro, according to sources who caution nothing on the matter is final until Trump says it.
In an Oval Office event earlier Monday, Trump said he was "very disappointed" in Pirro's decision to dismiss a felony indictment against three-time Olympian canoeist David Hearn last Friday. Pirro said in a 20-page filing that the damage was caused by "flawed installation by the contractor" and not vandalism as she and the president had long claimed.
Trump, however, continued to push allegations on Monday that vandals were responsible for cutting and tearing the pool lining. Trump said that Pirro "made a mistake" and "choked" under pressure from the judge in the case, later remarking that she "folded like an umbrella."
"The judge was extremely unfriendly to Jeanine. And frankly, I think she choked because the judge was really vicious. Instead of going after the people that did it, the judge went after her and went after her department and I guess she choked," Trump said.
Hearn was arrested at the Reflecting Pool in late June and charged with a felony for allegedly causing more than $1,000 in damage. Hearn said he had only touched a piece of the liner that was peeled from the bottom and pleaded not guilty to the charges.
In withdrawing the case, Pirro said new information indicated it was "difficult to attribute the widespread damage to the Reflecting Pool to vandalism." In particular, Pirro pointed to internal National Park Service communication from June 11 that raised concerns about the peeling pool liner more than a week before Hearn was arrested. Pirro also dropped misdemeanor cases against three other people related to destruction of property at the pool.
The president, who has long insisted that someone maliciously vandalized the lining of the pool with a knife or boxcutter, first rebuked Pirro's decision to drop the Hearn case in a Saturday social media post.
"I don't know what she was thinking? To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM," Trump wrote at the time.
The president deflected when asked on Monday if he would consider removing Pirro.
Even as he insists vandalism damaged the pool, Trump has also acknowledged the project's contractors might bear some blame for rushing to finish the project before the Fourth of July.
"So now I'm not saying I was 100% thrilled with the contractor, but the contractor was rushing. We wanted to get it open for July 4th, and we got it done. But in addition, there was vandalism," Trump said Monday.
Trump also alleged that Pirro assessed the damage in the immediate aftermath of the holiday, when strewn fireworks were "laying all over the pool." That claim contradicts Pirro's Friday court filing, in which she said she visited the pool on July 1.
The pool, which was drained for repairs shortly after the Fourth of July holiday, is currently empty and fenced off from the public. The president promised on Monday that it would be fixed and reopened in two weeks at most.
articles.summary: U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro met with President Trump at the White House Monday afternoon amid questions about her future, sources familiar with the matter told ABC News.

articles.title: ‘Game of Thrones’ author George R. R. Martin opens up about experiencing depression
articles.text:
George R. R. Martin, author of the wildly popular “Game of Thrones” book series, shared that he’s pulled back from updating fans via his blog as he “battled sadness and depression.”
“This year has been… stressful, to say the least,” Martin wrote in a blog post published this week, titled “Better Late Than Never.” “So much has been happening, it’s been overwhelming. Some great things, exciting things. Dreams coming true. But there have been nightmares too. I have lost friends. Battled sadness and depression.”
The entry marked Martin’s return to blogging since since Feb. 19. In his latest post, he thanked his “great staff of assistants,” who he said have worked tirelessly to keep him from “falling further and further behind.”
In recent years, the fantasy author has been called out by readers who complain about the delayed publication of the sixth “Game of Thrones” book, “The Winds of Winter.”
Martin addressed the criticism last year, writing in a May 2025 post that he “ought to get some other writer to pinch hit for me… I am going to die soon anyway, because I am so old. I lost all interest in ‘A Song of Ice and Fire’ decades ago. I don’t give a s--- about writing any longer, I just sit around and spend my money.”
In Monday’s post, Martin referenced his age again, writing, “The worst may be yet to come. I turned seventy-seven last September, and I tell you, getting old is no fun.”
He told fans that the combination of age and depression could mean his “posts are likely to [be] short and rushed” in the immediate future, adding that his “minions” may be helping him more.
But 2026 hasn’t been all sadness for the author, he said. In his post, he highlighted the nine Emmy nominations bestowed on his “A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms” on HBO Max.
Martin has won four Emmys, all as co-executive producer for “Game of Thrones.” The show won Emmys for outstanding drama series in 2019, 2018, 2016 and 2015.
This year’s awards show, which will air on NBC, takes place on Sept. 14 in Los Angeles.
“I hope to attend…” Martin wrote, “but that depends on… well, on a lot of things.”
articles.summary: George R. R. Martin, author of the wildly popular “Game of Thrones” book series, shared that he’s pulled back from updating fans via his blog as he “battled sadness and depression.”

articles.title: Embattled GOP Rep. Max Miller requests an Ethics investigation into himself
articles.text:
WASHINGTON — Embattled Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, said Tuesday he will request the House Ethics Committee to investigate domestic abuse allegations made by his ex-wife — an unusual move to try to exonerate himself amid a messy custody battle that is playing out in public view.
“In light of all the renewed interest in my family affairs I am going to file my own paperwork for an ethics investigation into myself to clear my name from these horrific attacks on myself and family. I have absolutely nothing to hide,” Miller, who has vehemently denied the allegations, said in a post on X.
“We will be providing the committee all necessary documents needed for a detail examination. The accusations continue to change, but my facts stay the same. I am looking forward to my colleagues reading everything for themselves,” Miller continued.
Rep. Miller vows to stay in reelection race amid abuse allegations
The two-term congressman did not say when he planned to ask the panel to probe the matter — such an investigation would likely take weeks, if not months. The House is out on its August recess and will return in September.
But the fact that he is making the request suggests Miller is not planning to drop out of his race for re-election, despite a declaration from his former father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno, a fellow Ohio Republican, that Miller is not fit to serve in Congress.
Earlier this week, Moreno issued a stunning statement saying Miller “needs serious psychological help” and is “a danger to my daughter,” Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, adding, “I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter.”
“If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them,” Moreno added. “He should not serve in the House of Representatives.”
In the Capitol on Tuesday, Moreno became emotional when telling reporters about the toll this public feud with Miller has taken on his daughter, granddaughter and wife.
“This is truly the seventh level of hell. This has been a horrific experience for my entire family,” Moreno said.
Moreno said his daughter lives in constant fear of Miller and said he met Miller at a police station on Sunday to pick up his granddaughter.
So far, President Donald Trump is standing by Miller, though the allegations are unsettling for some congressional Republicans. Trump on Monday called the situation “a very sad thing” and said Miller, a political ally, is a “good person.”
The president said he wanted to let the families figure things out.
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said the allegation that Miller engaged in domestic abuse is “none of my business. But the senator added: It just it doesn’t help. Just gives people more one more reason to be disgusted with Congress.”
Lawmakers typically do not request Ethics investigations into themselves, but it has happened before. In 2008, then-House Ways and Means Chairman Charlie Rangel, D-N.Y., asked the Ethics Committee to investigate allegations that he had improperly used congressional letterhead to rally support for an educational center named after him.
But the strategy backfired for Rangel. After a two-year Ethics probe, the panel found the longtime congressman guilty of violating 11 House ethics rules, and he was censured by the full House. Rangel had to relinquish his powerful Ways and Means gavel in the process, and he did not seek re-election in 2016.
articles.summary: Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, will request the House Ethics Committee to investigate domestic abuse allegations made by his ex-wife to try to exonerate himself.

articles.title: UFC fighter Allan Nascimento dies at 34 after apparent heart attack in his sleep
articles.text:
Brazilian MMA fighter Allan Nascimento died Monday after suffering a heart attack as he slept, the UFC said.
He was 34.
The “beloved flyweight fighter” was “found unresponsive after suffering an apparent heart attack in his sleep,” according to a statement from UFC.
“Despite the efforts of the responding medical team, he was pronounced deceased at the scene,” the UFC continued. “Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Allan’s family, friends, teammates, and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time.”
The 5-foot-8, 125-pound Nascimento went 22-7 in his UFC career that dates back to 2011.
He lost his last bout in a split decision to Mitch Raposo on June 20 in Las Vegas.
Nascimento’s sudden death stunned the mixed martial arts community.
“Today I lost a brother — a guy who was truly one of a kind — and the pain is unbearable,” No. 3-ranked lightweight and longtime friend Charles Oliveira said in a statement.
Brazilian middleweight Caio “The Natural” Borralho called Nascimento “one of the most kind fighters that’s I’ve ever met!”
“Polite, good energy and always in good spirits! He will be missed,” he said in a social media post.
And UFC correspondent Evelyn Rodrigues called Nascimento one of “the kindest souls I’ve ever had the privilege of knowing through MMA. Rest in peace, Allan.”
articles.summary: Brazilian MMA fighter Allan Nascimento died Monday after suffering a heart attack as he slept, the UFC said.

articles.title: Video shows moment drone burst into fireball on Russian beach
articles.text:
The beach was packed, many vacationers lounging near the turquoise waters when the drone slammed into the white sand and burst into a fireball.
Russian officials said seven people, including three children, were killed and 58 others injured by the explosion in the Black Sea resort town of Gelendzhik on Monday. The explosion was captured on video and shared on social media, and verified by NBC News.
Moscow accused Ukraine of targeting civilians, which would constitute a war crime, and unleashed a barrage of aerial strikes on its neighbor. Ukraine’s attacks inside Russia come as its own civilians faced deadly Russian bombardment throughout the summer.
Ukrainian officials did not confirm they were responsible, but they also did not deny it.
“What happened today was a deliberate strike by the Kyiv regime against the civilian population — people who have absolutely no connection to military infrastructure,” Veniamin Kondratyev, the governor of the Krasnodar region, said on his official Telegram channel. “There can be no justification for such a cynical and inhumane terrorist act targeting children.”
The explosion comes amid a concerted Ukrainian effort to push the war’s front line closer than ever to Moscow, with strikes targeting shipping vessels, oil sites, warehouses and ammunition depots in recent weeks.
Since Russian President Vladimir Putin launched his large-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Kyiv has honed an innovative and lethal strategy of using cheaply manufactured drones as it seeks to pressure Moscow into a peace settlement. Some hit their targets, while others are often shot down.
Between July 24 and July 31, at least 61 people were killed and more than 320 wounded in Ukrainian shelling and drone strikes, Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said Friday.
After the explosion in Gelendzhik, Andriy Kovalenko, head of the Ukrainian National Security and Defense Council’s Centre for Countering Disinformation, said: “Russian air defense shot down a drone onto people lying on the beach.”
“It was Putin who killed these Russians,” he said in a statement. “Had he not started the war and the strikes on Ukraine, they would be alive.”
Kovalenko also accused Putin of downplaying Ukrainian attacks on Russia, creating an “illusion of peace” that has made the public complacent.
“Had they acknowledged the war on their own territory, people would have reacted more actively to the alert, which in some places in Russia is not even announced,” he said.
A separate attack had also hit a warehouse in Leningrad, its regional governor, Aleksandr Drozdenko, said early Tuesday.
Ukrainian officials have said that Russian missile, drone and bomb attacks killed at least 377 in July alone, the highest monthly figure since April 2022, two months after the invasion.
Two children and an elderly woman were killed in the Sumy region from overnight strikes, the regional administration said early Tuesday. Two people were also killed in Zaporizhzhia, regional chief Ivan Fedorov said Tuesday, the same region where a day earlier he said one person was killed when Russia dropped eight powerful glide bombs.
Shipping vessels have also come under attack in recent weeks, often staffed by crew neither Ukrainian nor Russian.
On Tuesday, Turkey called on the warring countries to enhance navigational safety after a Turkish-owned vessel was hit, injuring some onboard. India made similar calls last month, condemning attacks on ships after its nationals were killed.
articles.summary: Russia and Ukraine traded blame after a drone slammed into a beach in the Black Sea resort town of Gelendzhik. Russian officials said seven people were killed.

articles.title: Trump claims Iran talks are underway as Tehran denies it
articles.text:
President Donald Trump accused Iran of duplicity and insisted the two sides were discussing reopening the Strait of Hormuz as early as Tuesday, even as Tehran denied talks were even taking place.
The diplomatic confusion was underscored by an attack on a cargo vessel near the strait’s Oman coast, as reported by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre, an organization run by the British navy that helps protect commercial shipping in high-risk areas.
With traffic through the bottleneck still at a trickle of its peacetime flow, the international oil benchmark Brent crude rose again by 2.7% Tuesday, reflecting uncertainty in the market rather than any confidence in the diplomatic process.
On Monday, Trump branded Iran “unbelievably duplicitous,” and accused it of asking for talks on ending the war only to announce no discussions would be held.
“They ask for a meeting, some would say ‘beg,’” he wrote on Truth Social. “Talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with ‘Oman.’”
In response to Trump’s claims of talks, Iranian Foreign Affairs Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters, “We currently do not have negotiations with America.”
Iran is in discussions with Oman over a temporary safe route through the strait, Baghaei said, adding it has no plans to host foreign delegations or send negotiators abroad in the coming days.
“We, of course, commend the Omani effort in aiding the mediation in this way. They have been taking a very important role and a significant role in the past couple of couple of weeks,” Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari told NBC News Chief International Correspondent Keir Simmons, who asked about the Omanis’ role during a news conference in Doha.
“Mediators in Qatar, Pakistan, and now Oman are all working together on that issue. We are coordinating very closely with the Omanis to facilitate the talks between both sides: exchanging ideas, exchanging drafts between between both sides,” he said.
Trump later told reporters at the White House that negotiations with Tehran were “going on right now.”
“It’s an amazing thing we have a little problem with Iran because we have many talks, and we’ll say we have or we don’t have. You know, we’re straight about it, but they deny it,” Trump said. “But they’re not denying it now. They just put out a statement not denying it.”
On the strait, he said the parties were discussing “having it open literally by tomorrow, completely open, and that’s phase one,” adding that the second phase of talks would focus on Iran’s nuclear program.
On Tuesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC, “There is a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait and move towards a more normalized position in this conflict.”
The president had earlier called off intense new strikes on Iran, giving space for what he said would be fresh negotiations.
Attacks have come the other way, though, with a cargo vessel reporting being struck by an “unknown projectile” on Oman’s coast Monday night, the UKMTO said. Maritime sources told Reuters on Tuesday that the vessel struck near Hormuz was a dry bulk ship. Its crew had to abandon the vessel and one seafarer was missing, the sources said.
Whereas in peacetime around 100 ships would pass through the strait in a day, at least six vessels passed through Monday, according to an NBC News analysis of MarineTraffic data.
Most of these, such as the Chinese-owned tanker Starway and the Indian-managed Horizon 1, continued to use the Iranian route which sees vessels sail south of Larak Island.
In the absence of an agreed safe route between Iran and Oman, some vessels are taking a chance traveling along the Omani coast, their transponders turned off so as not to broadcast their positions. The ship hit Monday evening was one of these, showing the risk still posed to those sailing through the strait.
articles.summary: President Donald Trump accused Iran of duplicity and insisted the two sides were discussing reopening the Strait of Hormuz as early as Tuesday, even as Tehran denied talks were even taking place.

articles.title: East Asia is baking in ‘cruelly hot’ summer
articles.text:
A deadly heat wave is gripping large parts of East Asia, bringing the hottest temperature on record in South Korea and complicating earthquake recovery efforts in Japan.
Extreme heat has been linked to 19 deaths in South Korea since mid-May, with President Lee Jae Myung calling it a national disaster Tuesday.
“We need to make efforts for a fundamental overhaul of the national crisis system, since this extreme weather is becoming normal,” he said at a Cabinet meeting.
On Sunday, temperatures hit 42.5 degrees Celsius (108 degrees Fahrenheit) in the southeastern city of Yangsan, the highest in 122 years of record-keeping.
While the abnormally high temperatures have mostly been concentrated in the south, in recent days they have spread north toward the capital, Seoul.
For the first time Tuesday, the Korea Meteorological Administration issued its new “severe” heat wave warning for all of Seoul after issuing it for parts of the city Monday. The warning is issued when the maximum perceived temperature is at least 38 C (100.4 F).
Residents of the Seoul metropolitan area, which is home to more than 26 million people, were advised to stay indoors, keep hydrated and check on vulnerable groups.
Temperatures are also soaring in North Korea, where the state newspaper Rodong Sinmun urged residents to avoid outdoor activities and farmers to protect their produce from the high heat, according to Yonhap.
Intense heat has also complicated disaster relief measures in Japan, where temperatures have exceeded 100 F since a 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Kumamoto prefecture on the southern main island of Kyushu on July 28.
More than 40,000 households are still without water, according to Japanese public broadcaster NHK, and thousands of people remain at emergency shelters while others are sleeping in their cars for fear of further powerful tremors.
Officials said Sunday that a woman in her 70s was found dead last week of apparent heatstroke while taking shelter in her car after the quake, bringing the total death toll to 38.
Calling the woman’s death “heartbreaking,” Kumamoto Gov. Takashi Kimura urged those who had been displaced from their homes to keep the air conditioning running in their cars or move to air-conditioned evacuation centers.
During a meeting Monday with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, he said residents’ lives had been made even more difficult by the “abnormal heat” and asked for greater government support to improve conditions at the shelters, many of which lack air conditioning and clean water.
Takaichi said the government was ensuring a “continuous supply” of water to evacuation centers, welfare and medical facilities.
“We will continue to work swiftly and thoroughly to restore services, including the repair of equipment in individual households,” she said while visiting an evacuation center in the town of Hikawa.
Elsewhere in Japan, officials at the Tama Zoological Park outside Tokyo said Monday that three lions had died in less than a week from suspected heat-related causes.
Officials said 10 of the zoo’s 16 lions had shown signs of distress starting in mid-July, including decreased activity and loss of appetite, with some losing consciousness or the ability to stand.
Despite efforts to cool their body temperatures, three female lions between the ages of 3 and 15 died within a week, officials said, the latest Sunday. Preliminary investigations found dehydration and multiple organ failure in all three lions.
While four of the zoo’s lions are in the process of recovery, three others remain sick, according to officials, who said that the animals’ health was their first priority and that they had been suspended from public display.
In an effort to promote awareness of the dangers of extreme heat, this year the Japan Meteorological Agency adopted a new name, kokushobi — or “cruelly hot day” — to describe days with temperatures over 40 C (104 F) after it received more than 200,000 votes in a public poll. The first kokushobi were recorded last month on five consecutive days.
The highest temperature ever recorded in Japan was last August in the city of Isesaki, at 41.8 C (107.2 F).
articles.summary: A deadly heat wave is gripping large parts of East Asia, bringing the hottest temperature on record in South Korea and complicating earthquake recovery efforts in Japan.

articles.title: Progress made in Strait of Hormuz talks, Rubio says
articles.text:
Live Updates: Rubio says progress made in Strait of Hormuz talks after Trump threatens "decapitation"
What to know about the Iran war today:
- Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that progress has been made in talks between Iran and Oman on the Strait of Hormuz, "but not finality yet," adding, "We're hoping that will happen very shortly."
- He made the comments after President Trump again backed down on attacks against Iran to allow for negotiations, saying, "I want to give them every last chance before decapitation. … We'll see what happens."
- Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis claimed Tuesday they carried out a drone strike on "a sensitive target" at an airport in southern Saudi Arabia. The Saudis have not commented on the claim.
Indian vessel sinks after being hit by projectile near Yemeni waters, official says
An Indian vessel sank Tuesday after it was hit by a projectile near Yemeni waters, according to an official.
The Indian MSV Faize Noore Oliya capsized after it was hit, and all 14 people who were on board, including 13 Indians, were rescued by the Yemeni Coast Guard, said India's Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways, in a post on X.
"India strongly condemns this unprovoked attack on the defenseless mechanised sailing vessel," he said.
Those who were rescued were brought to the Port of Mokha in Yemen.
Mediators working "to create the appropriate conditions" for direct talks, says Qatar
Qatar's foreign ministry said Tuesday that mediators in the U.S.-Iran conflict were "consistently working to create the appropriate conditions for the resumption of direct dialogue."
Countries in the Middle East were working collaboratively to avoid any new escalation in fighting, said Majed bin Mohammed Al Ansari, adviser to Qatar's prime minister and spokesperson for Qatar's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Al Ansari said in a weekly press briefing that Qatar, Oman and Pakistan have been "bending constant efforts to facilitate engagement" between the U.S. and Iran "to bridge their viewpoints."
Al Ansari also said Qatar is firm in its stance on freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, and that "the minimum demands at the current stage are to return to the previous status of the Strait, in line with international law and in coordination with all littoral and concerned nations," according to the foreign ministry.
U.S. job openings slip to 7.4 million, but labor market still resilient amid fighting
U.S. job openings fell slightly in June, but the labor market continued to show resilience in the face of economic shock from fighting in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Employers posted 7.36 million vacancies in June, down from 7.54 million in May, the Labor Department said Tuesday.
Openings dropped at wholesalers and manufacturers of nondurable goods. Openings rose by 97,000 at warehouse, transportation and utility companies and 39,000 at federal government agencies.
Layoffs were little-changed at 1.8 million, and the number of people quitting their jobs - a sign of confidence in their prospects - rose slightly.
Rubio says U.S. "involved in" Iran-Oman talks and that denuclearization is "ultimate deal"
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday the U.S. was "involved in" talks between Iran and Oman, and that Iran's denuclearization is the "ultimate deal."
Asked about the possibilities of a deal with Iran, Rubio said: "There's a big deal, which is the one that has to do with their nuclear ambitions. They can never have a nuclear weapon. So the denuclearization of Iran is the ultimate deal."
"I think the immediate deal, the one that there is focus on, is the Straits," he added, referring to the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb, two key Middle Eastern energy chokepoints that have been periodically closed by Iran and its Houthi allies over the course of the war.
"The Straits are open," Rubio said, repeating a line often touted by the Trump administration. "Nonetheless, I think that there's a conversation and a negotiation - that we are involved in - between Oman and Iran on how more ships can be able to go through there safely in the short term as we move towards the longer-term talks about denuclearization."
"Suffice it to say there's been progress made in those talks but not finality yet," he said. "We're hoping that will happen very shortly."
Rubio did not go into any specifics about U.S. involvement in talks.
Iraq exported 30 million barrels of crude via Strait of Hormuz in a month, says Kpler
Iraq exported over 30 million barrels of crude oil in one month through the Strait of Hormuz, data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler showed on Tuesday.
Before the Iran war, which choked shipments through the vital waterway, Iraq produced around four million barrels per day, and exported an average of 105 million barrels per month, mostly from its Basra oil terminal via the strait.
Around 30 million barrels of Iraqi crude oil passed through the waterway between July 4 and Aug. 4, according to vessels detected by Kpler.
Ali Nizar, the head of Iraq's State Organization for Marketing of Oil, said in a TV interview Monday that Iraq exported in July 35.5-37 million barrels via the strait.
Another seven million barrels were exported through an Iraq-Turkey pipeline to the Turkish port of Ceyhan.
Iraqi oil ministry spokesman Salim al-Rikabi told the state news agency INA on Tuesday that some tankers had passed through Hormuz after loading, adding that "the ministry is not responsible for their routes or the necessary approvals."
Crude exports normally account for about 90% of Iraq's revenues. They used to fill the state's coffers with up to $8 billion a month, but now they barely exceed $1.5 billion, oil minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair said last month.
Iraq, an OPEC founding member, was forced to halt production in most of its oil fields during the war as reservoirs filled up.
Due to the waterway disruption, it began exporting crude using tanker trucks through Syria, and a pipeline to the Turkish port of Ceyhan.
AFP
Iran will defend borders but doesn't want to expand war, says Iranian president
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tuesday that Tehran would defend its borders and interests but was not seeking to expand the war.
"We also defend our own limits and boundaries, but we are not seeking to expand the war or that we want to continue the war," he said during remarks at an official ceremony in Tehran.
Pezeshkian also stressed the importance of strengthening society internally to prevent external threats and interference.
"We must strive, in these circumstances, to create a society in which the enemy does not become tempted to infiltrate to tear apart and destroy our social fabric," he said.
Progress made in Strait of Hormuz talks, says Rubio, but no final agreement yet
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday "there's been progress made" in talks with Iran and Oman on the Strait of Hormuz, but that no final agreement has yet been reached.
Speaking to reporters at the State Department, Rubio said: "There's been progress made in those talks, but not finality yet. We're hoping that will happen very shortly."
U.S. stocks extend gains as oil prices fall more
Wall Street stocks rose early Tuesday, extending a rally following strong corporate earnings and comments from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Iran talks that pressured oil prices.
Bessent told CNBC that the U.S. could reach a deal with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz by Wednesday.
Iran has denied that the two sides are talking to resolve the more than five-month conflict and earlier U.S. statements signaling a likely imminent deal have proven overly optimistic, but oil prices tumbled on Bessent's statements.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1.3% - at 53,832.40 - about five minutes into trading. The broad-based S&P 500 gained 0.6% to 7,644.30, while the tech-rich Nasdaq Composite Index advanced 1.1% to 26,185.99.
The Dow on Monday finished at an all-time high on lower
