articles.title: Watch Live: Lindsay Clancy murder trial focuses on prescription pills
articles.text:
Watch Live: Lindsay Clancy murder trial focuses on prescription pills for Day 6 of witness testimony
The Lindsay Clancy murder trial resumed for a sixth day Tuesday with more testimony from prosecution witnesses and a focus on her prescriptions.
Clancy, 35, has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan — at their home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, on Jan. 24, 2023.
You can watch the trial live in the embedded video, on CBS News Boston or on the CBS News Boston YouTube page once testimony begins.
Testimony about Lindsay Clancy's prescription pills
Massachusetts State Police Lt. Joseph Rabbit said he found four prescription pill bottles in a kitchen cabinet when executing a search warrant at the Duxbury home after the murders. He said Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband Patrick Clancy and a lawyer came to the district attorney's office on Feb. 6 with more prescription pill bottles in a CVS bag.
Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham pulled out pill bottles one-by-one and asked about how many pills were prescribed compared to how many were left in the bottle. The prosecution has argued that while Clancy was prescribed several drugs for her mental health struggles, she was not taking many pills from each bottle.
The defense maintains she was overmedicated, and say a cocktail of several prescription drugs sparked a postpartum psychosis that led to Clancy killing her children.
"These were all pills that were issued on prescriptions in about a three-week period of time," defense attorney Kevin Reddington said in his questioning.
Crime lab workers testify
Several prosecution witnesses employed at the Massachusetts State Police Crime Lab took the stand on Tuesday. There was testimony about blood collected from the home in Duxbury - jurors were shown the blood-stained knife previously seen in Clancy's bedroom.
Two Crime Lab technicians also testified that prescription drugs were detected in blood and urine tests done on Lindsay Clancy. The tests are unable to pinpoint exactly how many different drugs Clancy had in her system, they explained.
South Shore Hospital surgeon testifies
The prosecution's first witness of the day was Dr. Cristina Karpio, a general surgeon at South Shore Hospital who treated Clancy immediately after the murders. She said Clancy's complex spinal injuries from her fall out of the second-story bedroom window required a transfer to Brigham & Women's Hospital in Boston.
Defense attorney Kevin Reddington asked Dr. Karpio about the severity of Clancy's injuries. The defense has tried to counter the prosecution's argument that Clancy's suicide attempt was faked.
"Did you know that your patient had coded shortly after being brought to Brigham & Women's hospital?" Reddington asked.
"No," Dr. Karpio said.
"Did you know that she had to have massive transfusions right after being brought to the hospital in Boston?" Reddington asked.
"No," Dr. Karpio said.
Lindsay Clancy agrees to "stipulation of facts"
Before the jury entered the courtroom on Tuesday, Lindsay Clancy agreed to a "stipulation of facts."
She was sworn in by a court officer and answered questions from the judge, confirming that she and the prosecution agree on certain facts in the case.
"This stipulation basically relieves the government of having to bring in dozens if not more witnesses to prove chain of custody of blood, fluids, the bands, DNA, all of that," defense attorney Reddington said. "Rather than have days of testimony, the stipulation will avoid that."
What's happened in the Lindsay Clancy trial this week?
The jury in Plymouth Superior Court heard entries from Clancy's diary Monday and testimony about her state of mind before and after the murders. She admits to killing her children but claims it was due to severe postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors say her suicide attempt was fake and premeditated and the murders were planned.
The jury has heard from 32 witnesses after five days of testimony.
If convicted, Clancy faces life in prison without a chance of parole. If she's found not criminally responsible for the deaths of her children, she will be sent to a state mental health facility in Massachusetts.
If you or someone you know is in emotional distress or a suicidal crisis, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. You can also chat with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline here.
For more information about mental health care resources and support, The National Alliance on Mental Illness HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m.–10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org.
articles.summary: The Lindsay Clancy murder trial resumed for a sixth day Tuesday with more testimony from prosecution witnesses and a focus on prescription pills.

articles.title: Behind closed doors, Trump, White House aides hope Rep. Max Miller exits race
articles.text:
Behind closed doors, Trump and White House officials hope Rep. Max Miller drops reelection bid, sources say
Washington — Some White House officials hope embattled GOP Rep. Max Miller exits the congressional race in Ohio immediately, and President Trump has expressed a similar sentiment behind closed doors, multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter tell CBS News.
Mr. Trump called Miller on Monday and raised concerns about his reelection bid following allegations that Miller assaulted his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and their 2-year-old daughter, two sources directly familiar with the call confirmed to CBS News. But Miller, who has adamantly denied the allegations, told the president he has no plans to leave the race, according to one of the sources.
Miller, the GOP nominee, has until 4 p.m. Wednesday to withdraw his candidacy and give Republicans a chance to replace him on the ballot in November. Semafor first reported that the president and some White House aides said privately that they wanted Miller out of the race.
On Tuesday morning, Miller said he would file the paperwork to launch a congressional ethics investigation into himself in an effort to clear his name.
"In light of all the renewed interest in my family affairs I am going to file my own paperwork for an ethics investigation into myself to clear my name from these horrific attacks on myself and family," Miller wrote on X. "I have absolutely nothing to hide. We will be providing the committee all necessary documents needed for a detail[ed] examination. The accusations continue to change, but my facts stay the same. I am looking forward to my colleagues reading everything for themselves."
On Monday, the president said he thought Miller was a "very good person" and said he would let the families involved resolve the situation.
"Well, it's a very sad thing," the president told reporters in the Oval Office Monday. "I know Max, he's a good person, I mean, I always thought he was a very good person. And I'm going to let the families figure that out. Those families, I know they're working on it. It's a very sad thing. Especially when you know somebody so well to be going through that. But it's accusations. And I'm going to let them figure that out."
In an earlier statement to CBS News on Monday, Miller said: "If I dropped out of this race, it would mean we as a nation have fallen so far from our American values. I will not validate false claims by removing myself just to please the court of public opinion. I am innocent of all of the allegations that have been attributed to me. I have done well representing my constituents' interests. Why would I drop out?"
Emily Moreno, Miller's ex-wife, is the daughter of Ohio GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno. The senator said in a statement on Sunday that Miller "should not serve in the House of Representatives" and "needs serious psychological help."
articles.summary: Some White House officials hope embattled GOP Rep. Max Miller exits his congressional race immediately, and President Trump has expressed a similar sentiment, multiple sources say.

articles.title: More adult children live at home now than during the pandemic
articles.text:
Record number of U.S. adults are moving in with their parents as costs rise, study finds
A record number of adult children under 35 in the U.S. are moving back in with their parents, either because they can't afford homes of their own or because they want to save money amid the rising cost of living, according to a recent study.
In 2025, 25.2 million adults under 35 lived at home, according to Realtor.com, which found that the share of adults living with their moms and dads was higher than it was during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Many of these adults moving back in with their parents are employed, but their wages aren't keeping up with inflation. Among the 25- to 34-year-olds living at home, roughly 7 in 10 have jobs, the online real estate firm found.
Karleigh Gaudreau, a 34-year-old business coach and online content creator, is among the Americans who recently moved back home, telling CBS News she couldn't afford to live on her own after breaking up with a boyfriend she had been living with in South Carolina.
Gaudreau, who earns about $60,000 a year, said she could afford to split rent but couldn't cover the full cost alone.
"To be able to afford that on top of your student loans or car payment, it's really hard to function off of anything, I believe, less than $85,000," Gaudreau said.
""Society as a whole has to respond"
She's hardly alone in her financial struggles, as the dream of homeownership slips further out of reach for many Americans amid rising home prices and higher mortgage rates. Fewer than 4 in 10 non-homeowner households can afford a typical starter home, according to a recent LendingTree analysis.
"Society as a whole has to respond," Susan Wachter, a professor of real estate at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School of Business, told CBS News. "It's affordability across the board. It's not just the price of the home and the mortgage."
Gaudreau's plan seems to be paying off. After saving money on rent by living with her parents, she plans to move into a place of her own in November.
articles.summary: One woman in her mid-30s said her $60,000 annual income wasn't enough to cover all her bills after a breakup, leading her to move back home.

articles.title: Eaton Fire in Altadena sparked by SoCal Edison electric tower, probe finds
articles.text:
California's Eaton Fire in Altadena sparked by SoCal Edison electric tower, Los Angeles County report finds
The Los Angeles County Fire Department on Tuesday released the conclusion of an 18-month investigation into the origins of the deadly and destructive Eaton Fire, determining that electrical arcing on an out-of-service transmission tower was allegedly to blame.
The report, conducted jointly between the LACFD's Arson Fire Investigation Unit and Cal Fire, determined that the arcing events "ejected hot metal particles that fell to the receptive fuel beds consisting of dry vegetation below the towers," which sits on a ridge above the Eaton Wash.
Starting Jan. 7, 2025, the Eaton Fire destroyed or damaged more than 9,000 homes primarily in the Los Angeles suburb of Altadena, and also affected nearby Pasadena.
The blaze took the lives of 19 people, according to the LA County Medical Examiner.
CBS LA reached out to Southern California Edison for comment, but did not immediately hear back. Last month, the utility company announced it paid more than $314 million to victims of the fire through its Wildfire Recovery Compensation Program.
articles.summary: The department said an 18-month investigation concluded that electrical arcing on an out-of-service Southern California Edison tower was responsible.

articles.title: Family "forever grateful" after 10-year-old rescued from rip current by teen lifeguard
articles.text:
10-year-old rescued from rip current by teen lifeguard says he thought he was going to die
A 10-year-old boy who was saved from a rip current off the coast of Santa Cruz, California, last month said he thought he was going to die before a 16-year-old lifeguard rescued him.
"I'm super thankful for him saving my life," Nathaniel Rai said about the teen lifeguard, Ryder Williams.
Nathaniel told "CBS Mornings" that "the waves were really big" that day at the beach so he stayed on the shore. But at one point he tripped and got pulled into the water.
"It was really quick and it felt scary because I didn't know if I was going to make it," he recalled.
Nathaniel's father, Sumit Rai, said his son was "a second or two away from dying" and he's "forever grateful" for Williams, who was the first person to respond.
"Ryder knew that if he lets go, Nathaniel is going to drown," Sumit Rai said. At that point, he said, Nathaniel was unconscious and not breathing.
"He just did everything he was supposed to do to save his (Nathaniel's) life and put himself at risk to do so," he said.
Sumit Rai also expressed gratitude for the other lifeguard who assisted and the good Samaritans who jumped in to help save his son.
"I appreciate each and every one of them, incredibly so, because, you know, it took that effort to bring him out and keep him alive. I'm just so grateful to have my son with me. I can't imagine what life would look like had Ryder not been there," he said.
In a statement last week, Ryder Williams said he too was grateful. "I'm grateful to have had the opportunity to return the child to his family safely. This is my job and I love what I do. I'm thankful to my fellow lifeguards who perform rescues just like this every day," he said.
Jake Shannon contributed to this report.
articles.summary: A 16-year-old lifeguard is being hailed a hero after rescuing a boy from a rip current off the coast of Santa Cruz, California, last month.

articles.title: Multiple passengers receive medical care after 22 flights diverted from Denver
articles.text:
Multiple passengers receive medical care after 22 flights diverted from Denver
(KXRM) – Multiple people required medical care after nearly two dozen flights were diverted in Colorado amid “significant turbulence” on Monday.
The Colorado Springs Municipal Airport (COS) confirmed that 22 aircraft, including four international flights, were diverted to the southern Colorado city from Denver due to severe weather.
Officials said “several passengers … [reported] medical concerns and required evaluation by emergency medical personnel” at COS. At least one passenger was taken to the hospital, Nexstar’s KXRM reported.
“Colorado Springs Airport remained open and operational throughout the event,” a spokesperson from COS Airport said. “COS and CSFD appreciate the coordinated efforts of airport personnel, airline partners, emergency responders and supporting agencies.”
The flights arrived between roughly 4:40 p.m. and 8 p.m. on Monday, but had all departed the airport by 10 p.m. local time.
Denver is considered one of the most turbulent airports in the country, and in some cases, it’s because of what are known as “mountain waves.” As air moves over the nearby Rocky Mountains, it can cause turbulent waves across the Eastern Plains, Nexstar’s KDVR explains.
When paired with thunderstorms, heat, or other weather patterns, it can make flights coming into Denver turbulent.
Routine turbulence may be annoying, but it typically isn’t dangerous. “Pilots handle that every single day. They know how to deal with it,” Dave Cunningham, director of operations at Denver International Airport, told KDVR last year.
There are cases in which it’s concerning, however.
A year ago, two people were taken to the hospital after their SkyWest flight from Aspen, Colorado, to Houston, experienced turbulence and dropped more than 4,000 feet in a minute.
Last summer, 25 people aboard a Delta Airlines flight from Salt Lake City to Amsterdam were taken to the hospital after their flight experienced serious turbulence and was forced to make an emergency landing in Minneapolis. Several passengers were not wearing seatbelts and were thrown around the cabin, a passenger said.

articles.title: Senate panel to vote on Fauci contempt resolution after tense hearing
articles.text:
The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (HSGAC) will vote Thursday on a resolution to hold former top health official Anthony Fauci in contempt following his hearing last week in which he invoked his Fifth Amendment right more than 100 times and refused to answer any questions.
The HSGAC will vote Thursday morning on the resolution regarding the “refusal of Dr. Anthony S. Fauci to answer questions pertinent to the subject under inquiry before the Committee as required by Committee subpoena.”
The resolution calls for Vice President JD Vance, who also serves as president of the Senate, to send the committee’s report of contempt to the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia.
In his appearance before the committee last week, Fauci made it clear at the start that he planned to answer no questions, stating his belief that committee Chair Rand Paul (R-Ky.) was using the proceedings as a way of somehow getting him “behind bars.”
Republican members of the committee both mocked and tested Fauci’s Fifth Amendment defense, with several insisting that he had no such protections due to former President Biden granting him a sweeping pardon. During the hearing, the argument over Fauci’s decision got to the point where one his attorneys, David Schertler, was removed from the room on Paul’s orders.
Paul acknowledged after the hearing that whether Fauci had Fifth Amendment protections was not clear, saying, “Maybe the Fifth Amendment doesn’t attach when you have a pardon in place.”
Prior Supreme Court rulings have maintained that witnesses need a degree of certainty on their immunity to overcome their constitutional protection.
The Hill has reached out to Fauci’s attorneys for comment on the planned vote.

articles.title: Will Congress finally stand up to California?
articles.text:
Will Congress finally stand up to California?
California Gov. Gavin Newsom is auditioning for the White House, trailing second among Democrats behind Kamala Harris according to the latest polls. Even though the roster for 2028 remains up-in-the-air, the Golden State’s chief executive is — in many ways — already acting the part. California is just 1 of 50 states, but routinely attempts to exert authority over the entire country.
Americans are not entertained.
A lawsuit filed in June against a California packaging law intends to loosen Newsom’s regulatory grip on the country. The legal drama is over the Plastic Pollution Prevention and Packaging Producer Responsibility Act, which limits single-use plastics and mandates that all packaging must be recyclable or compostable by 2032, among other rules.
Think you hate paper straws? Those flimsy, dissolving products were just the opening act.
California is free to experiment with foolish policies that impact Californians. Afterall, state voters have the power to hold their leaders accountable at the ballot box when ideas backfire. But such sweeping policies have ripple effects that extend beyond California’s borders. Companies — and their consumers — in any state that do business in California must comply.
“Once again, California is trying to enact a policy that negatively impacts the rest of the country,” said Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers when commenting on the problematic packaging rules. He warns that “if California goes unchecked, consumers will be forced to pay more for basic necessities.”
Holding California accountable in the courts is welcome, but the process can be arduous. Congress has the power to short circuit the legal proceedings and remedy the situation directly. A different saga unfolding in Washington over another attempt by California to regulate beyond its borders is acting as a trial balloon. Will lawmakers have the political appetite to go through with it?
Congress is currently debating an obscure California law called Proposition 12 that bans the sale of normal eggs and pork in Golden State supermarkets. Instead, consumers are limited to Whole Foods-style products at Whole Foods-level prices. Similar to the packaging statute, this strict animal agriculture standard impacts farmers in any state who sell pork or eggs in California.
Americans are expressing frustration with California’s edict because the policy is inflating food prices. It can cost millions of dollars for farms to retrofit facilities and adjust production systems to become California-compliant — a financial burden that rolls downhill to consumers at the checkout counter.
A bipartisan group of affordability-minded lawmakers is working to address the expensive domino effect as part of the farm bill. The House-passed version of the legislative package includes a food price fix that reins in California’s overreach. The provision confines Proposition 12’s enforcement to farmers within California.
More than a dozen House Democrats joined their Republican colleagues to make it happen. Even bitter rivals Presidents Donald Trump and Joe Biden agree that something needs to be done. Now, the ball is in the Senate’s court.
California is walking all over the rest of the country. Whether it’s micromanaging the design of packaging or banning certain foods from the dinner table, the efforts undermine the rights of people in other states. Congress needs to put a stop to it and focus on lowering prices for American families.
Jack Hubbard is the executive director of the Center for the Environment and Welfare.

articles.title: Max Miller says he will ask House Ethics panel to investigate domestic abuse allegations against him
articles.text:
Max Miller says he will ask House Ethics panel to investigate domestic abuse allegations against him
Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) on Tuesday said he will file paperwork to have the House Ethics Committee investigate him as he faces increasing pressure to resign or drop out of his reelection race over allegations of domestic abuse.
“In light of all the renewed interest in my family affairs I am going to file my own paperwork for an ethics investigation into myself to clear my name from these horrific attacks on myself and family. I have absolutely nothing to hide,” Miller wrote on the social platform X.
“We will be providing the committee all necessary documents needed for a detail examination. The accusations continue to change, but my facts stay the same. I am looking forward to my colleagues reading everything for themselves,” Miller added.
Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, has accused Miller of hurling scalding hot water at her, holding a gun to her head and breaking their daughter’s collarbone.
Miller has vehemently and repeatedly denied the allegations, and sued Moreno for defamation in May.
The two divorced in 2025 and have been engaged in a bitter custody battle over their daughter.
Even if the Ethics Committee does open an investigation, it’s highly unlikely the slow-moving panel would release a report ahead of November.
Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), Miller’s ex-father-in-law, over the weekend called for Miller to resign from office, arguing that he needs “to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake.”
On Tuesday, he said what his family had gone through was “the seventh level of hell.”
“This has been a horrific experience for my entire family. My daughter lives in constant fear of this man, not like something that’s existential, but deeply in her heart, she fears what this guy is capable of,” he said. “You can’t you can’t fathom what that makes me feel like when the dad’s number one job is to protect your kids. This has been brutal, beyond comprehension.”
“And if there’s any minimum standard for being an elected official, as I said, he fails to meet that minimum basic standard. I don’t care about the politics at all. Don’t think about it. Doesn’t enter my consciousness.”
Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) reportedly told MeidasTouch’s Pablo Manríquez that Miller should resign, while Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) told Manríquez that Miller “shouldn’t be in office.”
But other Republicans have been silent about whether Miller should drop out of his reelection race or face an ethics probe.
Asked whether he thinks GOP leaders should look into the allegations against Miller, Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio) said on “Face the Nation” that, “Well, again … this is an issue that is currently part of a divorce and part of litigation that’s in a courtroom, and the court should be handling this, which is clearly ongoing, and that’s where this needs to be, not in a television studio.”
Miller has repeatedly said he will not drop out of his race.
“If I dropped out of this race it would mean we as a nation have fallen so far from our American values. I will not validate false claims by removing myself just to please the court of public opinion. I am innocent of all of the allegations that have been attributed to me. I have done well representing my constituent’s interests. Why would I drop out?” Miller said in a statement to The Hill Monday.
Emily Brooks contributed to this report.

articles.title: Space X rocket on course to crash into the moon
articles.text:
A SpaceX rocket is on track to crash into the moon on Wednesday at 2:35 a.m. EDT.
The 8,800-pound SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket will collide with the moon at a speed of 5,400 mph, experts say. The impact will create a crater spanning approximately 89 feet, or 27 meters, wide.
The crash is expected to cause debris and dust to fall from the moon for several minutes but likely won’t be visible from Earth, according to the New York Times.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment on the matter, however, the company held a press conference on Monday about the expected occurrence.
SpaceX’s director of NASA Science and Dragon Programs, Julianna Scheiman, said the anticipated rocket crash stems from “a mixture of solar activity and gravity forces” that have put it on a “path towards the moon.”
She added that SpaceX is working with NASA and the other appropriate agencies on how to handle potential future rocket collisions with the moon, especially amid the presence of human astronauts.
Scheiman said the company is asking, “What is the best future disposal path for high-energy missions that are in the sun-Earth-moon system?”
The Falcon 9 rocket was launched on Jan. 15, 2025, in an effort to deploy two lunar landers.
One of them, named Blue Ghost, built by Texas based company Firefly Aerospace, successfully landed on the moon while the other named Resilience, built by the Japanese company Ispace, crashed into the surface.

articles.title: Self-identified 'liberal' Democrats rise in new polling
articles.text:
Self-identified ‘liberal’ Democrats rise in new polling
The Democratic Party has shifted to be more liberal over the past decade, with self-identified liberals now making up a majority of the party, according to a new survey.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll, released Tuesday ahead of Michigan’s closely watched Democratic Senate primary, found that 71 percent of Democrats now describe themselves as “liberal” — up from 55 percent in 2012. Meanwhile, the share of Democrats who lean “conservative” has fallen to 16 percent, down from 33 percent.
Liberal Democrats viewed higher taxes on the rich, universal healthcare and expanding access to abortion as the top three most essential political positions, according to the poll. Raising taxes on corporations and billionaires was the highest ranking essential position, with 76 percent of liberal Democrats placing it above all other policy positions.
The findings mirror a string of key primary victories by progressive candidates who have defeated more centrist rivals in the fight over the direction of the Democratic Party.
In Michigan, progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed is challenging Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) for the Democratic nomination to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) in a race that could determine whether the party’s increasingly liberal base can propel left-wing candidates to victory in battleground states.
The survey also found Republicans remain overwhelmingly conservative, though their policy priorities were less unified than Democrats’ view on key liberal issues.
Eighty-nine percent of Republicans identified as “conservative,” compared to 82 percent in 2012. Among conservative Republicans, 56 percent said reducing immigration is an essential conservative position, while 50 percent viewed shrinking the size of the federal government as most essential.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll surveyed 4,505 U.S. adults online over a period of six days, ending Monday. It had a margin of error of two percentage points for all respondents, and a margin of error of 3 percentage points for liberal Democrats and conservative Republicans.

articles.title: Grisham files restraining order against Max Miller
articles.text:
Grisham files restraining order against Max Miller
Stephanie Grisham, the White House communications director during President Trump’s first term, filed a restraining order against Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) on Monday, amid allegations that Miller abused his ex-wife.
Grisham’s counsel, Mark S. Zaid, announced on social platform X that they filed for a temporary restraining order against Miller as part of an ongoing lawsuit.
The case began with an op-ed Grisham wrote in 2021 in the Washington Post that described an abusive relationship with an unnamed man. Miller filed a defamation suit against her shortly after the article was published, but the case was eventually dropped as both parties signed a nondisclosure agreement to not publicly disparage one another.
Grisham filed her new lawsuit after Miller said in a June interview with Spectrum News that any allegations should be taken seriously and it “should be noted” that an allegation against him “came out on the same day as somebody’s book launch and the other part.”
“My ex-wife was with me every single day during that time of my life in that election, and she, in her own words, will tell you that I never did any of those things,” he added.
Miller is in a custody battle with ex-wife Emily Moreno over their daughter, a fight that has gained national attention as Moreno has accused Miller of hurling scalding hot water at her, holding a gun to her head and breaking their daughter’s collarbone. He has denied these allegations and vowed to continue his reelection campaign.
Moreno’s father, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), has publicly called for Miller to resign. Other Republicans have called for his resignation from Congress.
“First off, he shouldn’t be in office, right,” Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) told MeidasTouch’s Pablo Manríquez in a brief interview.
Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) also said in comments made to the outlet that based on what he knows, Miller should resign, stating that he has not heard the congressman’s side of the story but knows the Moreno family and he “can’t imagine they would go through this process if there wasn’t something there.”
Some Republicans are now wondering if there is time to replace Miller on the ballot, as the deadline for Miller to drop out is approaching. Democrats are eyeing the potential for an upset in a district Trump won by 11 points in 2024.
“I’m going to let the families figure that out,” President Trump said to reporters at the White House. “It’s accusations and I’m going to let them figure that out.”
On Tuesday, Miller announced on the social platform X that he would ask for an ethics investigation into himself in an attempt to clear his name.
“In light of all the renewed interest in my family affairs I am going to file my own paperwork for an ethic investigation to clear my name from the horrific attacks on myself and my family, Miller said.
“The accusations continue to change, but my facts stay the same. I am looking forward to my colleagues reading everything for themselves,” he continued.

articles.title: Talarico: Republican attacks on trans people 'culture war fights designed to tear us apart'
articles.text:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico said Monday that Republican attacks on transgender people are “culture war fights designed to tear us apart.”
“I mean, I don’t think we win by selling people out. And we’re refusing to do that in this campaign. This is a campaign of, by and for all Texans. And I think people are really tired of these culture war fights that are designed to tear us apart, designed to get us angry,” Talarico told MS NOW’s Rachel Maddow on her show.
“I mean, there are — there are difficult issues, trying to figure out trans athletes in sports, that’s an issue where we could actually come to a policy solution. But instead, politicians like Ken Paxton, they use those difficult issues to rile people up, to divide us, to distract us, in order to win power for themselves,” he added.
In recent years, the American right has increasingly focused on issues affecting the transgender community, such as gender affirming care and transgender people playing in sports categories aligned with their gender identity.
At the end of June, the Supreme Court ruled states can prohibit transgender girls from competing on girls and women’s school sports teams, keeping bans in Idaho and West Virginia in a 6-3 decision.
Talarico and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) are set to battle it out later this year for a Senate seat in the Lone Star State. Paxton has railed against transgender people playing sports in categories aligned with their gender identity, saying late last year that Talarico is a “left-wing lunatic obsessed with distorting Christianity to put boys in girls’ sports.”

articles.title: Appeals court blocks Trump from rescinding green bank funds
articles.text:
Appeals court blocks Trump from rescinding green bank funds
In a reversal, a federal appeals court has once again blocked the Trump administration from rescinding billions in climate funds issued under the Biden administration’s signature Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).
The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals reinstated part of a previous preliminary injunction that temporarily bars the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) from clawing back billions in “green bank” funding for climate-friendly projects.
Tuesday’s ruling came down from the entire bench of the circuit court. Previously, a smaller panel of appellate judges had canceled the injunction. It’s now back in place.
When he took office, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said he would recoup the $20 billion doled out by the Biden administration. The funds would go to green banks that would have awarded them to projects that aim to mitigate climate change or reduce pollution.
The Trump EPA, however, said that it terminated the program and sought to get the money back.
After the latest ruling, an EPA spokesperson said the agency was “reviewing the judgment and considering next steps.”
The spokesperson did not address The Hill’s request for a status update on the funds since the preliminary injunction was previously axed nearly a year ago.
The panel of judges said they were reinstating part of the injunction because the EPA’s move “likely contravened the IRA’s mandatory appropriation” since the decision was “based solely on a policy disagreement.”
However, some of the judges disagreed, saying the organizations that sued to get their money back did not show why the injunction was needed after Republicans repealed the section of the IRA as part of their “Big, Beautiful Bill.”
The Republican bill repealed “unobligated” funds from the program.
Meanwhile, one of the grantees, the Climate United Fund, celebrated the decision in a written statement.
“Today, the DC Circuit Court judges affirmed what we have always known: EPA took actions to unlawfully freeze and dismantle the National Clean Investment Fund grant program. Despite efforts to harm the awardees with false allegations and misinformation, there remains no legal basis for terminating our grant award and clawing back funds that were already disbursed in our bank accounts,” said the statement.
“As hardworking Americans grapple with an affordability crisis, the impact of the EPA’s decisions are far-reaching. This program was designed to lower energy costs, create good jobs, and improve public health. We will continue to pursue every legal avenue available to us to unfreeze funds on behalf of the communities we serve,” it continued.

Francesca Hong defends call to ‘cancel Thanksgiving,’ but says ‘views can evolve’
Democratic socialist and former Wisconsin state Rep. Francesca Hong (D) on Monday defended a past social media post urging the country to “cancel Thanksgiving” further leaning into her progressive agenda that’s gained traction for her Wisconsin gubernatorial campaign.
Hong, a professional chef, said Thanksgiving is a “time that’s incredibly painful for many people in our communities” during an appearance on CNN’s “The Source.”
“And so I think there I wanted to make sure that people understood that there are multiple views, but views can evolve,” she added.
Anchor Kaitlan Collins asked if Hong still stood by her now-deleted post on X from 2021.
“Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621,” Hong previously wrote on the social platform.
“If it takes a worldwide pandemic for us to realize we should stop celebrating colonialism and the original superspreader event that killed indigenous folx and women, so be it,” the post continued.
Hong responded by stating that, “I always think my hospitality background and owning a restaurant for seven, eight years that bringing folks around the table to share conversation and build community is always a good thing…I think my background as a chef will actually help me become a better governor that’s able to bring more people to the table.”
Republicans have been hammering Hong over the statement and the possibility of her becoming the Democratic nominee for governor in The Badger State.
“The Thanksgiving answer was so off the mark for what people view as ‘normal,'” Jessica Taylor of the non-partisan Cook Political Report wrote in a post on X.
Other strategists agreed.
“It’s answers like these than cause many to think if this chef wins the gubernatorial primary in WI, Ds may be cooked,” Democrat David Axelrod wrote in a Tuesday post on X.
Hong’s top competitor, former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes (D-Wisc.), suspended his campaign following allegations of sexual misconduct in the workplace.
Now Hong is facing off against Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, state Sen. Kelda Roys (D-Wisc.) and Joel Brennan in the Aug. 11 primary.
Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers (D) has endorsed Crowley while other Democratic progressives including Reps. Ro Khanna (Calif.) and Ilhan Omar (Minn.) are backing Hong, who has pushed for a state Economic Justice Bill of Rights and proposed a state bank and free social services.
However, Hong hasn’t received an endorsement from the Democratic Socialists of America but has gained support from several local chapters.
“Voters all across the state, regardless of party, want someone who’s going to be able to deliver change and deliver help to solve the problems that they have…,” Hong told The Hill on Tuesday, arguing that she’s just as “frustrated” and “stressed” over the current state of politics.
“So, what a democratic socialist and being a democratic socialist means to me is that I want the public goods. Childcare should be a public good, and public education, the services that everyone uses, from utilities to the roads. But I want them to be better for them. And being a democratic socialist means that I’m focusing on things being unapologetically pro-public,” she added.
The recent rise of democratic socialists in various primaries has brought some concern about how Democrats will perform in general elections. Establishment politicians argue that the new trend is localized and will not impact the national outcome in November.
However, socialists like New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) disagree, arguing that socialism is tied to the core values of the Democratic party.
“So much of what makes me proud to be a Democrat is looking at what our party used to stand for. You think about the Four Freedoms, you think FDR, you think the New Deal,” Mamdani told the New York Times in an interview.
“Those are at the core of what our party’s identity is, and yet it feels like to experience it, you have to read about it. You can’t see it around you anymore. And that isn’t something that I’m willing to accept, and I know that many feel similarly,” he added.

articles.title: Congressional conflict of interest: Why did the STOCK Act fail?
articles.text:
Congressional conflict of interest: Why did the STOCK Act fail?
Most congressional trades are just noise. One senator trims a tech position, while elsewhere a representative rolls a maturing bond and an adviser rebalances on schedule. It is the ordinary churn of money, and usually there is nothing to see. The work is sorting routine congressional trades from the occasional one that actually tells you something. Rep. Tim Moore of North Carolina just gave us one.
Last fall, and then again in March, Moore bought shares of LGI Homes, a builder of starter homes for first-time buyers. The stock was beaten up, trading near lows it had not seen in years. By itself, that would barely register. Members of Congress buy stocks all the time, but this one was different. Moore happens to sit on the House Financial Services Committee, one of the committees closest to housing policy and finance.
At the same time, Congress was moving a housing bill with unusually direct consequences for companies like LGI. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act cuts red tape for builders and pushes large institutional landlords out of parts of the single-family market. Fewer institutional buyers in existing homes can push demand back toward new construction. Moore voted for it, along with 357 colleagues, on June 23.
Since Moore began buying, LGI has risen from around $39 to about $55. A single purchase alone proves nothing, but Moore didn’t stop there. He kept adding, and this repetition is its own kind of tell. In markets, that usually tells you more than the first trade does. People average down for lots of reasons, but repeated buying into weakness often means they think the market is missing something.
Whether Moore knew the bill would pass is beside the point, because the votes were there. A lawmaker sitting this close to housing policy had every chance to read timing, substance and momentum better than everyone else. Even a small edge is still an edge.
When I buy or sell in my own account, the order goes to compliance first. Sometimes it clears and sometimes it does not. The principle is simple: If you might be in possession of material information, you should not be the only person deciding whether you get to trade on it. Congress works differently, letting members make that call themselves.
In school, the student does not grade their own exam. But that is effectively what Congress permits when members help shape bills and then trade the companies most exposed to them.
The STOCK Act was supposed to solve this. In practice, it mostly created paperwork. The penalty for filing late is $200, which tells you almost everything about how seriously it is treated by our elected officials. Set beside a portfolio reportedly worth around $9 million and more than 200 trades over three years, it is less a deterrent than a parking ticket. The rule in Congress has been trade what you want, disclose it later, and move on.
The market has adapted accordingly. Republicans cluster in banks, energy, defense and now crypto. Democrats cluster in big tech. Different sectors, but the same instinct to buy closest to the world you spend your days inside. This is what happens when the people with access and the people with capital are the same.
Moore’s own framing makes the trade harder to look past. He sold this bill as a leg up for first-time buyers chasing the American dream, while building a position in a company that stands to benefit when those same buyers are pushed toward new construction. That tension is not illegal, but it tells you something about the incentives at work. Since 2020, more than two dozen efforts to strengthen the STOCK Act have gone nowhere, because the people who would bear the cost of reform are the ones voting on it.
That leaves the work to everyone else. The filings are public, and anyone willing to put them beside the legislative calendar can see things the official machinery is not built to catch. Most of the time there is nothing there, but sometimes there is. And when it shows up, the trade usually exposes less about one member’s motives than about the system that made it ordinary in the first place.
Dan Weiskopf is portfolio manager of Subversive ETFs.

articles.title: Vivek Ramaswamy is struggling to connect with voters. Can Ohio’s Indian community help?
articles.text:
At the Hindu Temple of Dayton in south-west Ohio, there’s no little pride for gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy – he and his parents have been coming here to pray for decades.
On a quiet recent Tuesday afternoon, a priest lights incense sticks at the altar of the temple. Outside, a group of first-time visitors take a relaxed walk around the grounds.
“I remember him coming here with his parents when he was a little child,” saysAshwani Kumar, a priest from India’s Himachal Pradesh state who has served at the temple since the early 1990s, and says he intends to vote for Ramaswamy in November’s election.
“We are citizens, so we always support our [vote]. Real Hindu people believe in goodness,” he says. “Peace and goodness.”
Making up the largest immigrant group in the state, Ohioans of Indian heritage are set to see one of their own in Ramaswamy take center political stage ahead of the gubernatorial election this November. But their support for Ramaswamy, amid a rocky campaign, is not a guarantee.
For one, Indian Americans tend to lean Democratic. As of 2024, Pew Research Center found that 68% of the group identified as such.
But a smaller poll released in February by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace found that support slipping, with the number of people identifying as Democrat declining from what they say was 52% in 2020 to 46% this year. And more Indian Americans have appeared in the rightwing sphere, including in Donald Trump’s administration.
Harvard- and Yale-educated Ramaswamy, whose parents immigrated from Kerala before he was born in Cincinnati in 1985, himself received Trump’s much-coveted endorsement for Ohio governor in February 2025 – nearly two years before the election – to the shock of many in Ohio’s Republican establishment circles. Ramaswamy, who had run an unsuccessful campaign for president himself in 2024, then met little opposition in the Republican primary election last May, winning 82% of the vote.
But for a host of reasons ranging from xenophobia and outright racism from the right (a recent report found that Ohio’s classrooms are among the most segregated in the country) to accusations that he is a rich opportunist from the left, Ramaswamy, who made billions of dollars as a biotech entrepreneur, has struggled so far to connect with voters.
His difficulties have now led to pollsters at the Cook Political Report shifting the Ohio gubernatorial race from “leans Republican” to a “toss-up” this month, despite the state not electing a Democrat to the role for two decades and Trump winning Ohio by more than 11 points in 2024.
Ramaswamy created a major stir in December 2024 when appearing to criticize American workers, writing on X that, “Our American culture has venerated mediocrity over excellence for way too long … A culture that celebrates the prom queen over the math olympiad champ, or the jock over the valedictorian, will not produce the best engineers.”
His Hindu faith has also become a flashpoint on the trail. In a widely circulated clip from a Turning Point USA event last year, he attempted to answer a student who asked how he could represent a largely Christian state, while another asked him why he chose to “masquerade as a Christian”. Ramaswamy answered with an explanation of Hinduism and attempted to bridge the divide, calling himself an “ethical monotheist”.
In May, he struggled to offer a straight answer when asked by a television reporter in Youngstown to name his favorite place to stop by at in the city, responding: “I love long drives.” More recently, Ramaswamy was criticized for spending part of the Fourth of July holiday weekend in Paris.
“I think that Vivek, unfortunately, is out of touch from the struggles and concerns of the community – both the Indian American community, and the majority of Ohioans,” says Priya Tamilarasan, an attorney and Democrat based in the metro Columbus area whose parents immigrated from the state of Tamil Nadu in southern India decades ago.
“I think it’s very telling that, especially during the campaign cycle, especially during America 250 that he chose to focus on his own lavish lifestyle [by traveling to France]. Connection with and trusting the candidate requires deeper bonds than just someone that looks like you, or speaks the same language as you, or who has a name like you,” says Tamilarasan.
In January, an Ohio-based security person who worked for Ramaswamy was arrested on drug trafficking charges. Ramaswamy’s campaign team fired the security company that employed the bodyguard shortly thereafter.
Ramaswamy has little political experience, failing in his 2024 bid before quickly becoming a staunch backer of Trump, the eventual winner. He was briefly appointed to work with Elon Musk in creating the controversial Department of Government Efficiency but just weeks in.
This November, Ramaswamy is running against a fellow political novice, Democrat Amy Acton, who led Ohio’s response to the Covid-19 pandemic for several months in 2020.
Still, his national profile and entrepreneurial success have seen some among Ohio’s Indian community gravitate towards him.
Last November, the Ohio chapter of Americans4Hindus, a small political action committee (Pac), was formed and immediately endorsed Ramaswamy.
“The Indian American community in Columbus and across Ohio is strongly supportive – I’d say in the range of 70% to 80%. People are excited. They see Vivek as someone who understands both our cultural roots and the American Dream,” says Neil Patel, the Pac’s president.
“He’s a proud Ohioan, a successful entrepreneur, and a father who wants the same opportunities for every child that he and his family have been blessed with. There’s a real sense of pride and optimism in the community about what he can do for the state.”
“He has a clear, practical plan that speaks to what Ohio families actually care about – putting more money in people’s pockets and giving kids a world-class education,” says Patel.
An estimated 18,000 Indian immigrants live in metro Columbus, many who are students or faculty at Ohio State University, whose current president, Ravi Bellamkonda, is from Telangana in southern India.
In the wealthy suburb of Dublin situated north-west of Columbus, the 6,000-strong Indian American community is so prominent that local movie theaters show Bollywood films throughout the day. The Dublin Cricket Club has about 100 players, says Himavanth Ganta, a club board member who moved from Hyderabad to the US for college in 2012.
“It’s the sport that every Indian boy plays; it’s my passion,” he says. “We got our own cricket ground in 2016. Close to 70% to 80% of our members are people of Indian heritage.”
For him, when it comes to choosing a good political candidate, the character of the person outweighs their personal background.
“My friends say that [Ramaswamy] is someone to be proud of, being Indian,” says Ganta, who works in software for a large banking institution.
“I really don’t care what the candidate’s origin is. They have to do the right things for the people. Our priority is not to have an Indian as a governor; instead, we want them to take care of the people of Ohio.”
articles.summary: Ohioans of Indian heritage will see one of their own take center stage in race for governor, but their support amid a rocky campaign is not a guarantee  At the Hindu Temple of Dayton in south-west Ohio, there’s no little pride for gubernatorial candidate  Vivek Ramaswamy  – he and his parents have been coming here to pray for decades. articles.title: Ohio Republican Max Miller faces growing calls to resign over domestic abuse allegations
articles.text:
Max Miller, a Republican representative from Ohio, is facing a rising groundswell of resignation calls from his own party over domestic abuse allegations after his ex-father-in-law, Bernie Moreno, a GOP senator, said he was unfit to serve in Congress.
With a deadline looming for party leaders to choose a potential replacement, Miller, a former White House aide, also came under pressure from Donald Trump on Monday after the president reportedly called and told him “things aren’t looking good” for his re-election campaign against his Democratic opponent, Brian Poindexter.
Pleas for Miller to step down intensified after Moreno – father of Miller’s former wife, Emily Moreno – broke his silence on Sunday after months of refraining from comment on allegations concerning the alleged abuse of his daughter.
“If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them,” Moreno, an ally of Trump, posted. “He should not serve in the House of Representatives.”
Moreno’s comments came after Miller posted a livestream video defending himself against the abuse accusations and saying his former wife had “significant mental-health challenges”.
A series of public statements from Moreno’s fellow Republican senators indicate that their sympathies are with him.
“[Miller] should resign. He should quit,” Roger Marshall, a senator from Kansas, told Politico. “I don’t know Mr Miller’s story, but I trust Bernie [Moreno] so much as a good friend, and his family has such high values.”
The West Virginia senator Shelley Moore Capito said: “I don’t know [Miller]. I haven’t read a whole lot about him, but if [Moreno] thinks he ought to resign, I’m supportive of that.”
Lisa Murkowski, a Republican senator from Alaska, said: “The accusations are very serious, and if there is truth to them, I am one who says that our elected officials need to be held to high standards.
“And certainly, when it comes to allegations of domestic abuse, child abuse, that’s not what we want in our lawmakers.”
Three other senators, Rick Scott of Florida, West Virginia’s Jim Justice and Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming, also gave public backing to Moreno against Miller.
“I don’t know enough about the allegations, but like Bernie said, it sounds like he thinks he needs psychological help,” said Scott. “I trust Bernie.”
Miller – who married Emily Moreno at Trump’s club in Bedminster, New Jersey, in 2022 – has been accused of holding a gun to her head and scalding her with boiling water. Their toddler daughter, who was born in 2023, is also said to have suffered a broken collar bone due to his actions.
Miller denies allegations of abuse and has filed a defamation case against his wife over the claims. The couple divorced in 2025.
Axios reported that Trump called Miller on Monday amid concerns that the situation threatened Republican chances of holding the congressional seat in November’s midterms, when the party already faces an uphill challenge to keep its wafer-thin majority in the House of Representatives.
But the president avoided taking sides when asked about the issue by reporters in the White House. “I know Max, he’s a good person. I mean, I always thought he was a very good person. And I’m going to let the families figure that out,” he said.
Miller has resisted calls for him to withdraw from the race and told the Wall Street Journal that Trump “was supportive of me over the phone” on Monday’s call.
“He said he had a poll with no detail, and I pushed back with our poll that has us winning by 9 with our message out there,” Miller told the newspaper. “He kept on reiterating it’s going to be tough, and it’s going to be a really hard one for you.”
If Miller were to remove his name from the ballot before the close of business on Tuesday, a special Republican primary would be held to replace him.
If he were to withdraw after that, the party would still need to replace him by 10 August, but would need to give two days notice beforehand to hold a meeting to choose a substitute candidate.

articles.title: Todd Blanche’s attorney general nomination will advance to full US Senate vote
articles.text:
The US Senate judiciary committee voted along party lines to advance Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general after he confirmed in writing that a planned $1.8bn slush fund for Donald Trump’s allies was dead. Experts say, however, that Trump could easily reverse the deal.
His nomination will now proceed to the full Senate, where it will likely face intense skepticism from Democrats.
Ahead of the vote on Tuesday, every Democrat on the committee railed against Blanche’s nomination, saying he was unfit for the role and would do the president’s bidding. They emphasized his work defending the controversial fund, his mishandling of the files related to Jeffrey Epstein, the murder of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, and prosecutions of protesters and Trump’s political rivals.
“We are going to advance out of this committee probably the most discreditable person ever to seek the office of Attorney General of the United States,” said Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democratic senator from Rhode Island.
Blanche, one of Trump’s most trusted legal aides and formerly his personal defense lawyer, has faced questions over his suitability to lead the Department of Justice, which is supposed to operate independently of the White House.
He signed an order scrapping the so-called “anti-weaponization” fund – a roughly $1.8bn pool of money created in May as part of a settlement ending Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service – in a bid to defuse a Republican rebellion over his nomination.
The lawsuit came after the leak of the US president’s confidential tax records by a former IRS contractor, who has been serving a prison sentence since 2024.
Trump had cast the fund as compensation for people he claimed were unfairly targeted by politically driven investigations, and defended it as recently as this weekend. Critics said it risked becoming a taxpayer-funded payout to Trump loyalists, including some defendants from the January 6 Capitol riot.
The most consequential criticism stemmed from two Republican members of the judiciary committee, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina. Blanche’s nomination required their support.
But both outgoing senators have turned on Trump, recently telling party leaders they would not let Blanche’s confirmation move without firm guarantees that the fund would be shelved for good.
Speaking ahead of the vote on Tuesday, both Cornyn and Tillis said their concerns had been satisfied.
Tillis described the anti-weaponization fund as a “payout pot for punks”, but said he was satisfied it wouldn’t be moving forward.
“I’ve never liked this 1776 fund. It made no sense to me, and I thought it was an insult to the police officers and the people that defended us on January the sixth. It’s done. It’s been rescinded, and I am satisfied,” he said.
Despite saying he would vote for Blanche, Tillis lamented the politicization of the justice department under Blanche’s leadership. He criticized the department’s ongoing prosecution of the former FBI director James Comey in eastern North Carolina over a picture Comey posted with seashells arranged saying “86 47” – shorthand for getting rid of Trump.
“Some bonehead in North Carolina thinks that that’s a crime. Well, they better damn sure have information to back it up because if all it is is a picture, that person should lose his job, his or her job,” Tillis said.
Cornyn and Tillis faced public criticism from Trump over the weekend for pushing Blanche to put in writing that the anti-weaponization fund was dead and the scope of the tax immunity was limited. Cornyn defended the push on Tuesday.
“While this may sound like nitpicking to some, it’s critically important not only to me but to other members of the Senate,” Cornyn said. “Given this agreement with Mr Blanche, I expect the department to live up to to this in future litigation.”
Echoing the concerns of many other Democrats, Cory Booker, a Democratic senator from New Jersey, said the agreement with Blanche offered little assurance the justice department could not reverse itself and go ahead with the fund anyway.
“I’ve been here 14 years. I have not seen something as farcical as what I’ve witnessed over the last few weeks,” Booker said. “I’m going to say it very clear: this is all hat and no cattle.”
In his order, released on Sunday, Blanche stressed that the fund had never actually been operational: no board had been appointed, no money moved, and no claims filed or paid.
While there was concern that the settlement also provided broad immunity for Trump and members of his family from tax audits, the US Department of Justice separately clarified the IRS-related order was limited to the plaintiffs in the original settlement, and did not amount to blanket protection from future audits.
Both Cornyn and Tillis later confirmed they would vote to advance Blanche’s nomination.
Because the underlying settlement still references the fund, a future attorney general – or Trump himself, with Congress’s help – could try to revive it. Trump added to that uncertainty over the weekend, saying that if Blanche’s confirmation stalled, he would simply keep him on in an acting capacity and push lawmakers to create the fund through legislation instead.

articles.title: US federal judge blocks New York’s ban on ICE officers wearing masks
articles.text:
A New York law banning US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from wearing face coverings and requiring that they wear visible identification has been put on hold by a federal judge. But a state law prohibiting cooperation between local police departments and ICE has been allowed to stand.
The mask ruling comes after federal judges have blocked similar laws in California, Virginia and Pennsylvania that sought to ban federal immigration agents from covering their faces. They are still required to wear agency identification badges and badge numbers.
The US district judge Mae D’Agostino of the federal court in Albany, New York, wrote that while the state “appears to be well-intentioned in its pursuit of transparent policing”, her decision was made on constitutional arguments rather than “transparency or preferable policy decisions”.
D’Agostino said that New York officials “may be correct that federal immigration officers wearing masks and not displaying viable identification creates certain dangerous situations that the face covering and identification acts remedy”.
She wrote that the Trump administration nonetheless has shown a likelihood that the measures go against the supremacy clause of the US constitution, which bars state governments from regulating federal law enforcement.
The preliminary ruling means local police officers are blocked from arresting ICE agents for covering their faces in public settings.
“The United States has demonstrated a likelihood that it will succeed on its claim that [New York’s] face covering and identification acts directly regulate federal officers in violation of the supremacy clause,” D’Agostino wrote.
“Whether federal law enforcement agencies have chosen to carry out such operations in a sufficiently transparent manner is an important question. But that question is not for this court to answer at the present time.”
New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, signed the restrictions known as the “New York mask law” in late May in response to federal immigration enforcement tactics during Donald Trump’s second presidency. Members of the president’s Republican party argue that a mask ban undermines public safety.
On the issue of whether local law enforcement can cooperate with federal agents, D’Agostino’s 51-page preliminary ruling said New York’s ban on 287(g) cooperation agreements – which comes into effect later in August – should stand because it is an “appropriate means of furthering New York’s legitimate interests in protecting public welfare and choosing how state and local resources are expended”.
Brandon Neuman, a US justice department lawyer, argued in July that both the mask and cooperation bans in New York are invalid because states can’t make laws that regulate the actions of federal agencies.
“The key harm here is to the sovereign function of the United States,” he said.
James Percival, a general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees immigration enforcement agencies, reacted to D’Agostino’s ruling by saying on X that Democratic-led states “continue to stack losses as they try to pass unconstitutional bans on ICE officers wearing masks”.
Hochul and New York’s attorney general, Letitia James, said the ruling allowing the 287(g) ban to remain in effect shows the law “is legal and will keep our communities safe”.
“Local law enforcement should be focused on local matters, and New York taxpayers should not have to foot the bill for any collaboration with ICE,” they said in a joint statement.
“While the court enjoined enforcement of New York’s mask ban, we stand firm in our belief that masked agents do not make New York safer.”
The statement alluded to the New York government’s ability to appeal D’Agostino’s ruling, saying: “Our offices are reviewing all legal options at this time.”
ICE cooperation has become a campaign issue in Hochul’s bid for re-election in November. She is facing Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau county executive, who supports ICE tactics and opposes the prohibition of cooperation with the agency.

articles.title: Safety, freedom and no misgendering: inside the Texas summer camp for trans kids
articles.text:
For the first time in his life, 17-year-old Alastair Mendoza didn’t think twice about jumping in the water. He kayaked through tangles of reeds, taking in the schools of minnows beneath him and the hawks overhead. He splashed around with friends he had made only days prior.
“I actually felt comfortable,” Mendoza said of swimming in public, something trans kids like him often struggle with. But at Color Splash Out, a four-day summer camp open to queer and trans youth in Texas, Mendoza swam whenever he could. “There was less fear of judgment and anxiety knowing that you were safe around these people,” he said.
Led by Yadi Martínez-Reyna, a non-binary minister, Color Splash Out evolved from their inclusive religious practice into a secular, non-denominational space where LGBTQ+ kids like Alastair can play, create and connect without scrutiny.
“I wanted them to come and be themselves and have fun like you would at a regular summer camp, without the barriers of misgendering or feeling embarrassed or ashamed,” said Martínez-Reyna. “It’s about creating this space for self-esteem, self-reliance and self-empowerment, things they can take with them.”
Many of the attendees this year come from the Rio Grande Valley, a majority Latino region that is one of the poorest areas in the US. This is against the backdrop of a slew of anti-trans legislation and fear-mongering rhetoric in the state. Last year, Texas passed seven anti-trans bills, including a bathroom ban in government buildings, prohibitions on amending gender identity in certain records and the expansion of a 2023 ban on medical transition care for minors. Research has shown that LGBTQ+ youth who have at least one LGBTQ-affirming space report lower rates of attempting suicide. In the Rio Grande Valley, there are no queer youth organizations.
“There are not a lot of safe spaces,” said Nix Pasivan, 13, of their Santa Rosa hometown in the valley region.
Pasivan identifies as non-binary and their public school required them to cut their hair short, a traumatic experience they said they sobbed through. At camp, Pasivan said, “I’m so excited to be here, I just keep saying that, and I’m gonna keep saying it until mosquitoes start attacking me.”
At Color Splash Out, campers pay what they can, which means many pay nothing. The venue location changes every year due to safety concerns and a shoestring budget. Cabins, referred to as “houses” – inspired by ballroom culture and drag balls – are named each summer by campers. This year, houses included the Glitter Gorgons and the Rainbow Legends.
Besides participating in games and activities, campers also talk about the range of LGBTQ+ identities and skills for overcoming stress. At the beginning of camp, house leaders ask kids to share the names and pronouns they would like to go by while there.
“This is the first time I’ve ever heard someone say my name in public,” said Velvet, 11, who is non-binary and not out to most members of their heavily Catholic family. Their mother requested not to use Velvet’s last name for privacy.
Their parent, Ari Garza, who is non-binary and volunteered at the camp, worries about how Velvet will acclimate to starting middle school in the fall. A school-assigned therapist once told them to expect to be bullied.
Garza was one of several adults at camp who described the experience as meaningful, not just for the kids, but for them, too. “It’s like you’re healing your own inner child by making this happen for kids in this generation,” Garza said.
After ending a 20-year marriage with Velvet’s father, Garza came out as a lesbian, citing the need to set a strong example of bravery and break cycles of silence for Velvet and their older sister, who also identifies as a lesbian. “If I’m not brave enough, how are they going to feel safe?” they said.
Camp director Adora Ysaguirre said it’s the campers that inspire her. “I remember being intimidated by the confidence these kids had,” said Ysaguirre, about her first time at camp post-transition. “[Their confidence] is something I still pull from.”
Ysaguirre said she was doxxed and lost a teaching job in Boerne, Texas, for being trans. She has also faced harassment and multiple physical assaults. Eventually she took up sumo wrestling “to be able to take hits”, she said.
Ysaguirre said that kids often tell her she’s the oldest trans woman they have ever seen, and that they did not know it was possible to make it that far. “I have had a lot of heavy experiences … yet I’m still here … if somebody is struggling, I can sit with them and I can carry their weight with them, and it’s something I’m privileged to do.”
Color Splash Out invites former campers to become “fellows” once they turn 18 and help plan camps, fundraise and serve as a mentor to younger kids. House leader Cel Blanco understands how important it is to stay connected and supported – it’s why they keep coming back to volunteer at camp. They said when they aged out of their Dallas queer youth group and lost their community, they fell into an abusive relationship. “I know I’m not the only one,” they said. “It took so much to find me again.”
Since the federal funding cuts for non-profits, Color Splash Out has come to operate even more like a mutual aid project. Supplies were recycled from schools and personal use – this year, kids constructed group projects out of Frito-Lays boxes. Along the windowsills of the dining hall sat rows of banned young adult books in genres such as queer romance and social justice, donated by local school librarians who had to comply with conservative policies. The kayaks were lent by a returning camper’s mom who also volunteered as the camp’s nurse.
In order to make the camp happen each year, Yadi calls around for funding support from their network of religious leaders and regional connections. Three progressive reverends supported the camp this year; Yadi’s friends covered the rest of the costs. “It’s very grassroots, how we do things,” Yadi says. “I call it the little unicorn that could.”
After a last breakfast of migas, a Tex-Mex staple, Mendoza, Pasivan and Velvet took a van home, 8 hours south to the Rio Grande Valley. “When I came back,” said Pasivan the following week, “what I have to deal with felt a lot lighter, because now I understand more about it.”
Mendoza said he plans to become a Color Splash Out fellow next year. “Everyone made an effort to include people,” he said. “I didn’t really have that when I was first coming out … Everybody should have something like that.”

He kayaked through tangles of reeds, taking in the schools of minnows beneath him and the hawks overhead. articles.title: Man charged in Washington state with starting largest wildfire in the area
articles.text:
Authorities on Monday charged a man in Washington state with starting a wildfire that has consumed almost 4,000 acres and forced tens of thousands from their homes.
Aaron F Farinacci, 37, of Spokane, was arrested and charged with first-degree arson for setting the Old Trails fire, the largest of three devastating wildfires burning through the region.
He was found in possession of waterproof matches and a butane lighter – and was identified by witnesses who spotted him kneeling in grass close to where the blaze began over the weekend.
At a press conference on Monday night, John Nowels, the Spokane county sheriff, gave details of the suspect, including that he had a prior conviction in Arizona for manslaughter. According to the Phoenix New Times, the victim was Farinacci’s father, who was shot and killed at their Mesa home in 2010, reportedly after telling his son to do the dishes.
“As it happens in so many critical cases, it was citizens who were paying attention to their surroundings, being aware and willing to step up and say something that led to the relatively quick apprehension of Mr Farinacci,” Nowels said.
“This was fantastic, very quick work by everybody involved.”
Farinacci was expected to make his first court appearance Tuesday, Nowels said, as crews continued to battle the fires that have expanded across the county in recent days.
The Old Trails fire started Saturday north-west of downtown Spokane. The blaze jumped the Spokane river and ripped through neighborhoods that some residents were able to return to on Monday.
“There’s nothing to save,” said Miriam Sim, 76, as she and her husband, Daniel Sim, surveyed the ruined home where they had lived since 2005.
In one Spokane neighborhood, blackened vehicles, a boat twisted by the heat and melted plastic recycling bins remained. Across the street, lawns were still green and houses were spared, as residents continued to run hoses or sprinklers to water their properties.
More than 67,000 people were told to evacuate the three fires – Old Trail, Autumn Lane and Fairview – that by early Tuesday had burned about 16 sq miles (41 sq km) of Spokane, although orders in some areas were downgraded late on Monday.
Elsewhere across the state, where extreme high temperatures and a fourth year of drought conditions have taken hold, there were at least 15 wildfires burning, covering at least 390 sq miles.
Washington state’s entire congressional delegation wrote to Donald Trump on Monday urging the president to approve an expedited emergency declaration. Bob Ferguson, the state’s Democratic governor, said he spoke to the White House over the weekend after making his own emergency declaration.
“Hundreds of people have completely lost their homes and farms, and many are prohibited from returning to their homes or neighborhoods as crews continue to extinguish smoldering embers,” the politicians’ letter said.
No deaths or major injuries have been reported, although Cpl Mark Gregory, a spokesperson for the Spokane sheriff’s office, said Monday that 14 remained unaccounted for. They were, he said, probably people who had not been in contact since evacuating and were not truly missing or in danger.
More than 1,000 firefighters, many from out of state, arrived by Monday to help tackle the blazes, a number expected to double in the coming days, authorities said. Crews continued to fight the fires by land and air, with Nowels warning the public during the Monday press conference not to interfere with aerial operations by using drones.
A bulletin issued by the National Weather Service (NWS)’s Spokane office on Tuesday morning warned that challenging conditions would persist through the remainder of the week.
“Extensive amounts of smoke will continue over the region, maintaining unhealthy air quality,” it said.
“Dry conditions and breezy winds increase Friday and Saturday across portions of central Washington, bringing elevated fire weather conditions.”
Hundreds of homes, businesses, and other structures have been destroyed in what Dave Upthegrove, Washington’s commissioner of public lands, called “an extraordinary wildfire season across the Pacific northwest”.
The Associated Press contributed to this report
